t.codrul secular sinca@45.7,25.2:
Codru is an old Romanian word for a deep forest, and the Codrul Secular Șinca, the ancient forest of Șinca, is exactly that: a stand of old-growth beech and fir on the northern slopes of the Făgăraș mountains in Brașov county, where trees have grown, died and fallen for centuries without being cut. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the ancient and primeval beech forests of Europe, a chain of protected forests across many countries that together tell the story of how beech spread across the continent after the last ice age. Walking among trees that are hundreds of years old, with fallen trunks covered in moss and fungi and the canopy closing high above, is a humbling experience.

Nearby, at Șinca Veche, is one of the most mysterious places in Romania: a temple carved into the sandstone of a hill, with chambers, niches and carved symbols, whose origins are unknown and the subject of much speculation. It is now a small Orthodox monastery, and visitors come for its atmosphere and the legends surrounding it. The Făgăraș mountains, rising to the south, are the highest in Romania, and the famous Transfăgărășan road crosses them further west.

The riding in this area is good. The main road between Brașov and Făgăraș runs along the foot of the mountains, with long curves and views of the peaks, though it can be busy with trucks. Side roads into the villages and the foothills, toward Șinca Nouă and Poiana Mărului, are quieter and more scenic, with meadows, forests and haystacks. The road from Zărnești to Bran and the Rucăr-Bran pass, with views of the Piatra Craiului and Bucegi mountains, is one of the most beautiful in Romania. Watch for horse carts, sheep and dogs, and beware of bears, which are common in the forests of this region.

Zărnești, about seventeen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and it is the gateway to the Piatra Craiului national park. Făgăraș, to the west, has a large medieval citadel. Local food includes hearty soups, grilled meats, and cheeses from the mountain shepherds, often wrapped in fir bark, which gives them a distinctive flavour. Try papanași, fried doughnuts with sour cream and jam.
t.village of viscri@46.1,25.1:
Viscri is the village people picture when they think of Transylvania's Saxon heritage, and it more or less lives up to it. A single long street of pastel houses, blue, ochre and white, stands gable end to the road, with geese in the ditch, horse carts at dusk and, at the top of the slope, a fortified church wrapped in thick white walls. It is part of the Villages with Fortified Churches in Transylvania listed by UNESCO, and it is one of the best preserved.

The Transylvanian Saxons, German-speaking settlers invited by Hungarian kings in the Middle Ages, built these church fortresses to survive raids from the Ottomans and Tatars. Each family had its own storeroom inside the walls, where bacon, grain and valuables were kept, and when danger came the whole village retreated behind them. Climb the tower and you can see the wooden galleries and the views across rolling pasture and woodland. After 1990 most Saxons emigrated to Germany, and the villages emptied. Viscri's revival owes a lot to conservation groups and to King Charles III, who bought and restored a house here and has long championed the place.

Today you can buy knitted woollen socks and felt slippers from village women, sometimes straight from a doorstep, and the home-cooked meals in guest houses lean towards soups, smoked meats and fruit preserves.

The village lies a few kilometres off the main road between Sighișoara and Brașov, reached on a side road from Bunești. Ride it slowly. The point here is to arrive gently: cows walk home on their own in the evening and know they have right of way. The surrounding hills are gentle, mostly grazing land and oak woods, and the main road nearby carries heavy truck traffic, so the side roads through the Saxon villages, Saschiz, Biertan and others, make a better way to link the area. Some of those lanes are rough, so check the surface before committing a heavy bike.

Rupea, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel and shops and its own hilltop fortress worth a look. Arrive in the late afternoon, when the light warms the house fronts and the street smells of hay and woodsmoke.
t.sanpaul cetate@46.2,25.4:
Sânpaul, Homoródszentpál to its Hungarian-speaking inhabitants, is a village in the Homorod valley in Harghita county, in the heart of the Székely Land of eastern Transylvania. Near the village, the Romans built a fort on the eastern edge of their province of Dacia, guarding routes through the hills from the Carpathians. The remains, now earthworks in the fields, are part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, listed by UNESCO in 2024. Nearby Ocland has a medieval fortification on a hill known as Hășmaș castle.

The Székelys are a Hungarian-speaking community with a strong sense of identity, and their villages are distinctive. Look for the carved wooden gates in front of houses, massive structures with roofs, decorated with flowers, inscriptions and symbols, built to show the family's status. Many villages have fortified churches, Unitarian, Reformed or Catholic, with walls and towers built for protection in times of trouble.

The Homorod valley is gentle countryside, with rolling hills, meadows, orchards and forests. The region is famous for its mineral water springs, called borvíz, which bubble up naturally and are drunk straight from wells in many villages. Some are slightly fizzy, some taste of iron or sulphur, and locals swear by their health benefits. In the hills above the valley, the small spa of Homorod Băi has wooden villas and springs.

The riding here is a pleasure. Roads wind along valleys and over hills, through villages and forests, with views of the Harghita mountains to the east. Traffic is light, and surfaces on the main roads are mostly good, though minor roads can be rough. Watch for horse carts, cattle being driven home in the evening, and dogs. Brown bears are common in the forests of Harghita, sometimes coming close to villages, so take care at dusk and do not leave food around.

Fuel is limited in the villages. The nearest larger settlement listed is Mugeni, about fourteen kilometres away, and Odorheiu Secuiesc, the main town of the area, lies a little further. Try a kürtőskalács, a chimney cake baked on a spit and rolled in sugar and cinnamon, or a hearty bowl of goulash, and wash it down with fresh mineral water from the village spring.
t.rasnov cumidava la cetate@45.6,25.4:
The Roman fort of Cumidava stood on a terrace near the village of Vulcan, just west of Râșnov, at the southern end of the Bârsa Land, guarding the route from Transylvania through the mountains to Wallachia. It was one of the forts on the eastern frontier of Roman Dacia, and its name, recorded on an inscription, is believed to be Dacian in origin. The site is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, added to the UNESCO list in 2024. Little stands above ground, but the setting, with the mountains rising to the south, makes it clear why the Romans chose this spot.

Râșnov itself is dominated by a peasant citadel on a hill above the town, a fortress built by the Saxon villagers in the Middle Ages to protect themselves from raids. Inside the walls, houses, a school and a chapel were built so that families could live there during sieges. A deep well in the courtyard, according to legend, was dug by Turkish prisoners over many years in exchange for their freedom. The view from the citadel over the Bârsa plain and the mountains is superb.

A few kilometres south lies Bran Castle, marketed as Dracula's castle, though its connection with Vlad the Impaler is tenuous. It is crowded, commercial and fun, perched on a rock above the road. Beyond Bran, the road climbs over a pass to Câmpulung, through the villages of Moieciu and Fundata, with meadows, haystacks and views of the Bucegi and Piatra Craiului mountains, one of the most beautiful landscapes in Romania. Brașov, the main city of the area, has a charming medieval centre and the Black Church, the largest Gothic church in the region.

The riding is excellent, with mountain roads, passes and villages, and plenty of bends. The roads around Bran can be congested with tourist traffic, especially on weekends. Surfaces are mostly good on main roads, more variable on minor ones, and livestock and dogs are common. Bears are present in the forests and sometimes come close to towns, so take care.

Vulcan and Râșnov have fuel and shops, and Brașov has everything. Try a plate of mici, grilled minced meat rolls, or a bowl of bean soup served in a bread bowl, with a glass of local beer after the ride.
t.village of darjiu@46.2,25.2:
Dârjiu is a Székely village of around eleven hundred people in Harghita county, and at its heart stands one of the fortified churches that UNESCO lists among the Villages with Fortified Churches in Transylvania. Most of those villages are Saxon and Lutheran; Dârjiu is Hungarian-speaking and Unitarian, which makes it something of an odd one out and all the more interesting. A ring of thick walls and towers encloses the church, built so that villagers could shelter from raiders, and the tradition of storing smoked bacon and grain in the fortress towers lasted here long into modern times.

Inside, the church is known for its medieval wall paintings from the early fifteenth century, including scenes of the legend of Saint Ladislaus pursuing a Cuman warrior, a story that turns up on walls across the old Hungarian kingdom. The paintings survived partly by luck, under later whitewash, and they are worth the small effort of finding whoever holds the key. Ask in the village; someone usually knows.

Riding in, you come through the rolling uplands between Odorheiu Secuiesc and Sighișoara, a landscape of low hills, beech woods and huge open pastures where shepherds still move flocks between villages. The roads are mostly narrow county tarmac with patched surfaces, some potholes and the odd stretch of gravel on the shortcuts. Horse carts are common, and so are cows that consider the road theirs. Take it gently and you will enjoy the rhythm of crests and dips, with a church tower marking each village.

Mugeni, five kilometres away, is the nearest place of any size, and Odorheiu Secuiesc, further north, has fuel, banks and proper restaurants. Look out for kürtőskalács, the chimney cake baked on a spit, and for the carved Székely gates in front of the farmhouses. If your ride continues to Biertan or toward Sighișoara, you will be crossing from Hungarian to Saxon heritage within an hour, and Dârjiu, with its bacon towers and its painted knight, is the perfect counterpoint to the grander Saxon churches you will see later.
t.hoghiz la cetate@46.0,25.3:
Where the Olt river bends around the Perșani mountains, between the Saxon villages of southern Transylvania and the Székely country to the east, the land rises into wooded hills, and near the village of Hoghiz, on a terrace above the river, lies an archaeological site known simply as La Cetate, the fortress. The Romans guarded this stretch of the Olt with forts, part of the defensive system of their province of Dacia, and the name hints at an old fortified place that once watched over the valley.

The area is geologically remarkable. A few kilometres north, at Racoș, an extinct volcano has left columns of basalt, dark hexagonal pillars exposed in an old quarry, and a small crater lake nearby. The Olt cuts a narrow gorge through the hills here, and the landscape is a mix of forests, meadows and villages. To the west lies Rupea, with a medieval Saxon fortress on a basalt hill, restored and open to visitors, from which there are wide views over the surrounding countryside.

The main road from Brașov to Sighișoara passes nearby, a busy route with heavy trucks and frequent overtaking, so choose minor roads where you can. The country lanes along the Olt and through the villages are quieter, though surfaces vary and potholes are common. Horse carts, sheep and dogs share the roads. The hills around offer some winding stretches, and the views across the valley to the Perșani mountains are fine. Summer is warm, autumn beautiful, and winters cold with snow.

Hoghiz is a small village with basic services, and Rupea, eight kilometres away, is a town with fuel and shops. The Saxon villages around, such as Viscri and Saschiz, have fortified churches and offer guesthouses and traditional food. Try ciorbă, a sour soup, and papanași, fried doughnuts with sour cream and jam. In the evening, the light on the hills and the river is soft, and the sound of sheep bells drifts across the valley from the pastures.
t.ibanesti cetatuia mica@46.8,25.0:
Up the Gurghiu valley in Mureș County, the villages still wear wood: carved gates, shingled roofs, little wooden churches and stacks of firewood against every wall. Ibănești is one of the best known of them, a long village strung along the valley where traditional dress, music and crafts have hung on more stubbornly than in most of Transylvania. On a hill nearby, Cetățuia Mică, the little citadel, marks a point on the eastern frontier of Roman Dacia, where a chain of small forts and watchtowers looked toward the volcanic Gurghiu mountains and the lands beyond. These eastern posts are part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing for Dacia, added by UNESCO in 2024, though on the ground they are grassy earthworks rather than walls.

Above Hodac, the neighbouring village, a mountain fair has been held for generations, traditionally a gathering where young people from the valleys met, courted and, so the story goes, arranged marriages. Today it is more of a folk festival with music and dancing, and it gives a taste of how isolated mountain communities kept their social lives turning.

The riding up the valley is a gentle climb along the river, through villages and meadows, with the forested slopes closing in as you go. Surfaces are mostly decent on the main valley road but can turn rough higher up, with potholes and gravel, and forestry roads into the Gurghiu mountains are best left to proper off-road machines. Horse-drawn carts, cows walking home in the evening and children on bicycles are part of the traffic.

Ibănești and Hodac have small shops and bars, and Gurghiu, about eight kilometres down the valley, is a little larger. For a sure tank and a supermarket, head for Reghin, the market town at the mouth of the valley, which is famous for its violin workshops; instruments made there are sold around the world. Food in the valley is homely: sour soups, smoked bacon, polenta with sheep's cheese and pastries filled with cheese or cabbage.

Late spring brings meadows full of flowers and fresh green beech woods, and autumn turns the forests copper. Winter here is long and snowy. The valley has a slow, unhurried rhythm, and the best way to enjoy it is to match it: ride at a walking pace through the villages, nod back to the old men on the benches, and leave the stopwatch at home.
t.voinesti mailatoaia@45.3,25.1:
The Rucăr-Bran corridor is one of the oldest passages through the Carpathians, and at its southern end, in the hills around Câmpulung Muscel, the Romans built a frontier line to guard it. The Limes Transalutanus, the frontier east of the Olt, ran north through this area, and small forts and watchtowers like the one at Voinești-Măilătoaia watched the valleys and the approaches to the pass. The sites are now low earthworks in fields and forest edges, and they belong to the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing for Dacia, added by UNESCO in 2024.

Câmpulung, a few kilometres away, was the first capital of the principality of Wallachia in the fourteenth century, and its old princely church and monastery are among the oldest religious buildings in the country. The surrounding hills, the Muscel, are dotted with villages, orchards and woods, and the people here are known for their strong traditions and fierce attachment to the land.

The road north from Câmpulung toward Bran is one of the classic rides of Romania: it climbs through Rucăr and the Dâmbovicioara gorge area, winds over the pass at Giuvala and drops toward the castle of Bran, often marketed as Dracula's castle, with views of the Piatra Craiului ridge, a long sharp limestone crest, and the Bucegi mountains. The road is twisty, scenic and well surfaced, but busy with trucks and tourists, so pick your moment. Side roads into the villages are quieter, narrower and rougher.

Voinești and Valea Mare Pravăț are small villages with a shop or two. Câmpulung has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Rucăr, further up the valley, has fuel and accommodation. Local food is mountain fare: polenta with cheese, sour cream and fried eggs, grilled meats, trout from the mountain streams and pastries with sweet cheese.

Come in late spring, when the orchards are in blossom and the meadows full of flowers, or in autumn, when the forests blaze with colour and the apples ripen. Summer brings warm days and afternoon storms, and winter makes the high roads icy. Ride the corridor slowly, stop on the pass to look back toward the plains of Wallachia, and you will see why travellers, traders and soldiers have used this route for two thousand years.
t.baraolt veczer@46.1,25.6:
In Baraolt you are more likely to hear Hungarian than Romanian. This small town lies in Covasna County, in the heart of the Székely Land, where the Székely Hungarian community has lived for centuries, with its own traditions, carved wooden gates, Calvinist and Catholic churches and a fierce sense of identity. Véczer, near Baraolt, is one of the points on the eastern frontier of Roman Dacia, where small forts and watchtowers watched over the passes through the eastern Carpathians, and it belongs to the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing for Dacia, added by UNESCO in 2024.

The landscape around Baraolt is a mix of rolling hills, forests and small valleys, with the Baraolt mountains to the north and the Olt river winding through a gorge to the west. Near the village of Racoș, a short ride away, the remains of an extinct volcano have left columns of basalt and a small crater lake, a striking geological curiosity in the middle of the Transylvanian countryside. Lignite was mined around Baraolt for decades, leaving its mark on the town.

The riding here is relaxed and pleasant, with roads winding through hills, forests and villages, light traffic and generally decent surfaces, though potholes and patched sections are common on smaller roads. The Olt gorge near Augustin is a scenic stretch, where the river cuts between wooded hills. Watch for horse-drawn carts, livestock and pedestrians in villages, and for logging trucks on forest roads.

Baraolt, about five kilometres away, is a small town with fuel, shops and restaurants. Augustin and Căpeni are small villages with basic services. Food in Székely Land is Hungarian-influenced: goulash, paprika chicken, chimney cake, the sweet spiral pastry roasted over coals, and hearty soups with smoked meat. Local mineral water, from the many natural springs in the region, is excellent and often free from roadside wells.

June, with its hay meadows, and September, with its harvest, show the Székely hills at their best. Summer brings warmth and festivals, winter snow and cold. Ride slowly through the villages, admire the carved Székely gates with their inscriptions and decorations, and enjoy a corner of Romania where two cultures, and a Roman frontier, meet in quiet hills.
t.village of saschiz keisd@46.2,25.0:
The clock tower of the fortified church in Saschiz looks oddly familiar if you have just come from Sighișoara, and that is no accident: it was built in the image of the famous clock tower of the nearby town, a statement of local pride by the Saxon villagers who built it in the late fifteenth century. The church belongs to the World Heritage inscription for villages with fortified churches in Transylvania, a group of German-speaking Saxon communities that fortified their churches against Ottoman and Tatar raids. Above the village, on a wooded hill, are the ruins of a peasant citadel, where the inhabitants took refuge during attacks.

Saschiz, called Keisd in German, is a village of about two thousand, on the main road between Sighișoara and Brașov. Most of the Saxons emigrated to Germany after 1990, and the village is now mainly Romanian and Roma, but the houses still have their colourful facades and big wooden gates. The village is known for its blue-painted pottery, a tradition revived in recent years, and for local products such as jams and syrups made from wild fruits. The surrounding countryside is one of the most beautiful in Europe, with meadows full of flowers, ancient oak pastures and wildlife including bears and wolves.

The riding is a pleasure, but with a catch. The main road through Saschiz is a busy international route, full of trucks, and needs care. But the side roads to villages such as Viscri, Criț and Mesendorf are quiet, winding through hills and valleys, some paved, some gravel. The surface on minor roads can be poor, so take it easy. Spring and early summer are the best seasons, when the meadows bloom. Fog lies in the valleys in the morning, and summer brings thunderstorms. Winters are cold.

Saschiz has a few shops, guesthouses and a café; for reliable fuel, Sighișoara, about twenty kilometres away, is the safe choice. Food here mixes Romanian and Saxon traditions, with soups, stews, smoked bacon and cakes. Many guesthouses serve home-cooked meals with local ingredients. Climb up to the citadel for the view over the village and the hills, then visit the church, whose painted interior is a surprise after the austere exterior.
t.pauleni dealul silas@46.4,25.2:
Corund is a village where almost every house seems to sell pottery. Stalls line the main road through this Székely community in Harghita county, piled high with plates, jugs and bowls in white, blue, green and brown, painted with flowers and birds. Pottery has been made here for centuries, using local clay, and the craft is still alive, though much of what is sold today is made for tourists. Păuleni and the hill called Dealul Silaș lie nearby, an archaeological site among many in this land of rolling hills and forested ridges, with little to see on the ground.

The Székelys are a Hungarian-speaking community who have lived in eastern Transylvania for centuries, and their villages, churches and customs give this area a distinct character. You will see carved wooden gates, Székely gates, at the entrances to many farmyards, with intricate patterns and inscriptions. The signs are bilingual, and Hungarian is spoken more often than Romanian.

Nearby are some of the most interesting sights in Transylvania. The salt mine at Praid, a few kilometres to the west, is huge, with caverns big enough to hold sports fields and playgrounds, and the air is said to be good for respiratory problems. Sovata, a little further on, is a spa town built around Lacul Ursu, the Bear Lake, a salt lake that traps heat in its layers of water, so that the water below the surface can be surprisingly warm. Odorheiu Secuiesc, to the south, is a pleasant town with churches, a fortress and a lively centre.

The riding is excellent. The road from Sovata through Praid and Corund to Odorheiu Secuiesc winds through hills, forests and villages, with good surfaces and a mix of fast bends and tighter sections. Side roads climb into the Gurghiu and Harghita mountains, where the forests are thick and the air smells of pine. Watch for logging trucks, horse-drawn carts and the occasional bear; brown bears are common in these mountains, and they sometimes come close to roads and villages, especially in the evening.

Corund has shops and bars, and Odorheiu Secuiesc has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Try kürtőskalács, a sweet spiral pastry baked on a spit over coals, sold at stalls in the area. Spring and autumn are lovely; winters are cold and snowy.
t.ocland cetatea hasmasului@46.2,25.5:
The Homoród valley runs south through the Székely land of Harghita county, a gentle, green valley between wooded hills, with villages of whitewashed churches and carved gates. Ocland is one of them, a small village with a fortified church, and on a hill above it stood a medieval castle, Cetatea Hășmașului, of which only traces remain. The rides that pass here connect it with the fortified churches of Transylvania, the extraordinary defensive churches built by the Saxon and Székely communities in the Middle Ages to protect themselves from Tatar and Ottoman raids.

Some of the finest of those churches lie within easy reach. Viscri, a Saxon village to the southwest, has a fortified church with white walls and towers set on a hill, part of the UNESCO site of the Villages with Fortified Churches in Transylvania, and the village itself, with its colourful houses and unpaved streets, has become famous. Closer at hand, the Székely villages of the Homoród valley have their own fortified churches, smaller but no less charming.

Nature is also a highlight. The Vârghiș gorge, to the east, is a narrow limestone canyon with dozens of caves, some of them inhabited in prehistoric times. Băile Homorod, further north, is a small spa resort in the forest, with mineral springs and wooden villas. The forests here are home to brown bears, wolves and deer, and you may see bear warning signs on the roads.

The riding is pleasant and varied. The road through the Homoród valley is gentle, with long straights and easy bends, while the side roads climb into the hills, with steeper gradients, tighter corners and rougher surfaces. The roads through the forest are quiet and beautiful, especially in autumn, when the beech and oak turn gold and red. Watch for gravel, potholes, livestock and horse-drawn carts.

Ocland is a small village with basic shops; for fuel and full services, head to Odorheiu Secuiesc, to the north. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer can be hot, and winter brings snow and ice. Local food is hearty: try goulash, cabbage dishes or a plate of fresh cheese with polenta. Take a moment at a fortified church, walk around the walls, and imagine villagers sheltering inside as raiders swept across the hills.
Southeast of Sfântu Gheorghe, in Covasna county, the plain of the Râul Negru, the Black River, opens out between the mountains, a broad basin of fields, meadows and villages enclosed by the forested ridges of the Eastern Carpathians. Boroșneu Mare is one of the larger villages in this basin, a Székely community with a church and a cluster of farms, and the hill above it, Dealul Cetății, the Fortress Hill, takes its name from old earthworks or a fortification recorded there. It is one of many such sites in the area, more a landmark than a monument.

This corner of Transylvania is known for its mineral springs and mofettes, natural vents of carbon dioxide used for therapeutic baths. The town of Covasna, a short ride to the east, is a spa town with dozens of springs, and the gas-filled mofette rooms are a curious experience. Further north, Bálványos is a small resort in the forest, close to the ruins of an old castle and to Lake Sfânta Ana, a perfect crater lake in the Ciomatu volcano, the only one of its kind in Romania.

Nearby, at Reci, there is a surprising sight: a patch of sand dunes in the middle of the Transylvanian countryside, now partly covered with birch woods and protected as a nature reserve. It is a strange and lovely place for a short walk.

The riding in the basin is easy and flat, with long straights and wide views of the mountains on all sides. The roads that climb into the hills, towards the Bodoc mountains to the north or the Întorsura Buzăului pass to the south, are more interesting, with bends, gradients and forest. Surfaces vary; the main roads are generally good, but minor roads can be rough. Watch for horse-drawn carts, livestock and dogs, and be aware that bears live in the forests and are sometimes seen near roads.

The nearest towns with full services are Sfântu Gheorghe and Târgu Secuiesc, both with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Brașov, one of the most beautiful cities in Romania, is less than an hour away. The weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters; the basin is known for its cold, foggy winter mornings. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.church of the assumption of the virgin o:
The painted monasteries of Bukovina are among the most extraordinary buildings in Europe, and the Church of the Assumption of the Virgin at Humor, just outside Gura Humorului in north-eastern Romania, is one of the finest. Built in 1530 and painted inside and out a few years later, it belongs to the group of churches that were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1993. The outer walls are covered with frescoes in rich shades of red and brown, telling biblical stories and lives of saints to people who could not read.

The most famous scene at Humor is the Siege of Constantinople, painted on the south wall, which mixes the Persian siege of the seventh century with the more recent Ottoman threat. It was a political message: the Moldavian princes who founded these monasteries saw themselves as defenders of Christianity against the Ottomans. The church was founded by a Moldavian nobleman, and the monastery buildings around it, with a defensive tower and walls, show how monasteries also served as refuges in times of war.

Bukovina is a land of rolling hills, beech and spruce forests, wooden farmhouses with carved gates and neat haystacks in the fields. Voroneţ, with its famous blue frescoes, is a few kilometres away, and Suceviţa and Moldoviţa are within easy reach. The Slătioara old-growth forest, one of the last virgin forests in Romania, lies to the west.

On two wheels Bukovina is hard to beat. DN17 runs from Suceava through Gura Humorului towards Câmpulung Moldovenesc and Vatra Dornei, with curves through valleys and over hills. Minor roads to the monasteries and villages are narrower and sometimes rougher, and you will share them with horse-drawn carts. The road over the Ciumârna pass between Moldoviţa and Suceviţa is a classic, with tight bends and great views. Watch out for dogs, potholes and slow traffic.

Gura Humorului, six kilometres away, is a small town with fuel, hotels, restaurants and shops. Bukovina cuisine is hearty: ciorbă rădăuţeană, a sour soup with chicken and cream, sarmale and papanaşi, fried doughnuts with cream and jam. The monasteries welcome visitors, but modest dress is expected, and nuns may ask you to cover shoulders and knees.
t.reci cetate@45.8,25.9:
Reci lies on the flat floor of the Târgu Secuiesc basin, in Covasna county, where the Olt river meanders between mountains in the heart of the Szekler Land, the Hungarian-speaking region of eastern Transylvania. The site known as Reci - Cetate, the fortress, belongs to the eastern line of the Roman frontier in Dacia, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire inscribed in 2024. The Romans guarded the passes through the Carpathians with forts and towers here, though today the site is little more than a raised area in the fields.

What makes Reci unusual is its natural setting. Near the village lies a small nature reserve of sand dunes and birch woods, a strange landscape of hollows and hummocks covered with heather, birches and marsh plants, a remnant of conditions after the last Ice Age. It is a very different world from the surrounding fields and mountains, and well worth a short walk.

The Szekler Land has a strong identity. Villages have tall carved wooden gates, Hungarian is the main language, and churches are often fortified, like the famous one at Prejmer near Braşov, a World Heritage Site, with its massive circular walls and hundreds of storage rooms for villagers under siege. Sfântu Gheorghe, nine kilometres away, is the county capital, a pleasant town with a strong Hungarian character.

Riding in the area means flat valley roads with long straights, surrounded by mountains on all sides. The roads into the mountains, through passes towards Braşov, the Buzău valley or the spa towns of Covasna, are curvy and scenic, with forests and rivers. Traffic is moderate, and the roads are generally in good condition, though villages bring the usual hazards of dogs, horses and slow vehicles.

Sfântu Gheorghe has fuel, workshops and restaurants. Try kürtőskalács, the chimney cake baked on a spit and rolled in sugar, and hearty dishes like goulash or stuffed cabbage. The region is also famous for its mineral water springs, and many villages have their own spring where locals fill bottles. A picnic by a spring, with bread, cheese and fresh water, is a simple pleasure.
t.olteni castelul miko@46.0,25.8:
The Olt here is a young river, winding through meadows in the basin north of Sfântu Gheorghe before it bends west across Transylvania. At Olteni, a village on its banks, the Mikó family, one of the noble houses of the Szekler Land, had a manor house set in a park, and the place is linked to one of the Roman sites of the eastern Dacian frontier listed in 2024. The Romans had a fort in this area, guarding the routes through the mountains, and like most sites in the region, little of it can be seen today.

The Szekler nobility built manor houses and small castles across this region, many of them now in various states of repair. The Mikó family is also associated with the castle in Miercurea Ciuc, further north. Olteni's manor reflects a time when these families were the leaders of local society, and the parks and gardens around them were their pride.

Nearby Bodoc is famous across Romania for its mineral water, bottled from springs in the hills, and Malnaş has a small spa with mineral baths. The region is full of such springs, and you can often stop to fill a bottle with fresh, naturally sparkling water. North of here, the Olt passes through the Tuşnad defile, a narrow valley between volcanic mountains, and the spa town of Băile Tuşnad, with Lake Sfânta Ana in a volcanic crater nearby.

Riding in the area is easy and pleasant. The main road along the Olt follows the valley with gentle curves and good surfaces, while side roads into the mountains offer more challenging bends and forest scenery. The road to Lake Sfânta Ana is a beautiful climb through forest, ending at the crater rim. Bears are common in these mountains, and in some places they come close to roads, especially in the evening. Never feed them and keep your distance.

Sfântu Gheorghe, twelve kilometres away, has fuel and services. The local food is Szekler and Hungarian: goulash, paprika chicken, stuffed peppers and chimney cakes. In the evening, a glass of local wine or a shot of pálinka in a village inn is the perfect way to end the day.
t.campulung jidova 1@45.2,25.0:
Câmpulung Muscel lies at the foot of the Carpathians in northern Argeș county, and it claims the title of the first capital of Wallachia. Tradition credits its founding as a princely seat to the legendary Negru Vodă in the thirteenth century, and the old princely court and the Negru Vodă monastery in the town centre recall those early days of the Romanian principality. The town spreads along the valley of the Râul Târgului, with the mountains of Iezer and Piatra Craiului rising steeply to the north.

On the southern edge of town, at a place called Jidova, lie the remains of a Roman fort, one of the northernmost points of the Limes Transalutanus, the frontier line the Romans built in the early third century east of the river Olt. The fort guarded the route north toward the mountain passes into Transylvania, and its stone walls have been excavated and partly displayed, making it one of the more visible Roman sites in the region. It forms part of the ensemble of Roman frontier sites in Romania nominated for UNESCO listing.

That same route is the reason most riders come here. North of Câmpulung, the DN73 climbs through the Rucăr-Bran corridor, a high, open passage between the Bucegi and Piatra Craiului mountains, with villages scattered across alpine meadows and views of jagged limestone ridges. Along the way, the Dâmbovicioara gorge offers a detour into a narrow canyon, and the road eventually descends to Bran, home of the castle marketed as Dracula's, and on to Brașov. The road is well surfaced, with long, flowing curves, though trucks and summer weekend traffic can be heavy.

The hills around Câmpulung are also known for their orchards and their traditions. The town's surroundings produce apples, plums and walnuts, and the villages along the corridor are famous for sheep farming, with cheeses like brânză de burduf, sheep's cheese packed in bark or skins, sold at roadside stalls.

Câmpulung, a town of over thirty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants; Schitu Golești and the other nearby villages offer basic services. Try a plate of local trout or grilled meats, and enjoy the cool mountain air after the heat of the plains. The best time to ride the Rucăr-Bran corridor is from late spring to early autumn, when the meadows are green and the passes are clear of snow.
t.campul cetatii cetatea sacadat@46.7,25.0:
In the eastern part of Mureș county, near the boundary with Harghita, the hills rise towards the volcanic mountains of the Eastern Carpathians, and the villages are mostly Hungarian-speaking. This is part of the Székely Land, home to the Székelys, a Hungarian-speaking people who settled here in the Middle Ages to guard the eastern frontier of the Kingdom of Hungary, and who maintain a strong identity, with their own runic script, carved wooden gates and fortified churches. Câmpul Cetății, the field of the fortress, is a village near Eremitu, and the site of Cetatea Săcădat is one of the elements of the Roman frontier listed by UNESCO, on the eastern edge of the province of Dacia, where the Romans built a line of forts and towers along the foothills of the mountains.

Sovata, about ten kilometres away, is a spa resort famous for its salt lakes. The most remarkable is Lake Ursu, the Bear Lake, a heliothermal lake: a layer of fresh water on top of salty water traps the heat of the sun, so that the water a metre or so below the surface can be much warmer than at the top. Bathing in it is a strange experience, and it is popular for its supposed health benefits. The resort has wooden villas, parks and forests.

Nearby Praid has one of the largest salt mines in Romania, with vast underground chambers used as a treatment centre and recreational area; you can descend by bus into the mine and spend time in the salty air. The whole region sits on a huge salt deposit, and salt springs and salt rocks appear on the surface in places.

The riding is excellent. The roads from Sovata into the mountains climb through forests with tight bends, and the road over the Bucin pass towards Gheorgheni is a classic, with long bends, good surface and views over the mountains. The minor roads between villages are narrower and more variable. Watch for livestock, carts and wildlife, including bears, which are common in the forests of the Eastern Carpathians.

Sovata has fuel, shops, hotels and restaurants. Try kürtőskalács, chimney cake, a sweet pastry cooked on a spit and coated with sugar, sold at stalls everywhere in the Székely Land, and a bowl of goulash soup.
t.residence of bukovinian and dalmatian me:
The Residence of the Bukovinian and Dalmatian Metropolitans in Chernivtsi is one of the most extraordinary buildings in Eastern Europe, a red-brick complex of towers, domes and arcades that looks like a cross between a Byzantine monastery, a Moorish palace and a Victorian college. It was designed by the Czech architect Josef Hlávka and built between 1864 and 1882 as the seat of the Orthodox metropolitan of Bukovina and Dalmatia, then provinces of the Austrian Empire. The roofs are covered with coloured glazed tiles in patterns derived from the folk art of the region, the interiors are lavishly decorated, and the complex includes a seminary, a church and gardens. Today it houses the Chernivtsi National University, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2011. Students fill the courtyards, and guided tours show the main halls, including the stunning Marble Hall.

Chernivtsi was the capital of the Austrian crown land of Bukovina, and in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, it was a remarkably cosmopolitan city, with Ukrainians, Romanians, Germans, Jews, Poles and Armenians living side by side, and a lively cultural scene in German. It was often called Little Vienna, and its centre, with a theatre, cafés and Art Nouveau buildings, still recalls that era. The poet Paul Celan was born here in 1920, as were many other writers and artists, and the city's Jewish community, once a large part of the population, was largely destroyed in the Holocaust.

After the First World War, the city became part of Romania, then in 1940 it was occupied by the Soviet Union, and today it is part of Ukraine, a short distance from the Romanian border. Its history of changing borders is visible in its architecture and its people.

The riding in the area is varied. The roads into the Carpathian foothills to the southwest, towards Vyzhnytsia and the Cheremosh valley, are scenic and winding. The surface ranges from good to poor, with potholes common.

Chernivtsi has fuel, mechanics and plenty of restaurants. Try banosh, cornmeal porridge, and varenyky, filled dumplings. Ukraine is at war, and although Chernivtsi is far from the front lines, air raid alerts occur across the country; check the current official travel advice very carefully before considering any trip, and follow local instructions.
t.church of the annunciation of the monast:
Moldovița is the monastery that makes people go quiet in the courtyard. It sits in a green pocket of the Bukovina hills, ringed by a stout defensive wall with corner towers, and inside it the Church of the Annunciation is painted from the ground to the eaves with saints, prophets and battle scenes in blues, reds and ochres that have survived some five centuries of Carpathian weather. It was founded in the time of Petru Rareș, in the 1530s, and it belongs to the famous group of painted churches of northern Moldavia that UNESCO lists together.

The paintings were never decoration alone. They were a Bible for a congregation that mostly could not read, and the outside walls tell the stories in sequence. Look on the southern wall for the Siege of Constantinople, a crowded scene with Moldavian and Ottoman anxieties folded into a Byzantine subject, and for the long Tree of Jesse, which tangles the ancestors of Christ in a vine. The monastery is lived in, with nuns working in the grounds and a small shop that sells their weaving and woodcarving, so cover your knees and shoulders, speak quietly, and avoid using a flash on anything inside.

Getting here is half the pleasure. The valley road climbs from the Moldova river past Vama and Câmpulung Moldovenesc, through villages of steep shingled roofs and haystacks propped on poles, and the corners are gentle enough that you can look at the hillsides while you ride. Traffic is mostly local cars and the occasional timber lorry, and the asphalt is generally fair, though patched in places after winter. A small mountain road crosses the saddle toward Sucevița, another of the painted churches, and it makes a good loop if the day allows. Early morning is best, before the tour coaches arrive, and the beech and spruce woods are at their finest in October when the slopes turn copper.

Moldovița village and Vatra Moldoviței both have guesthouses, cafés and small shops, and you can buy a bowl of ciorbă, sour soup, or a plate of mămăligă with sour cream and cheese without trouble. For fuel, plan on Vama, about sixteen kilometres off, or Câmpulung beyond it; the villages in the immediate valley are small and I would not count on a pump. Leave yourself an hour. The place rewards anyone who stays longer than the usual ten minutes.
t.eremitu dealul tompa@46.7,25.0:
You are in Szekler country here, in the hills between the Niraj valley and the foot of the Gurghiu and Harghita mountains, a part of Transylvania where most villages have two names and the Hungarian one, Nyárádremete for Eremitu, is the one people use. Dealul Tompa means the blunt hill, and it matches the landscape: rounded, grassy and farmed, with beech woods on the higher ground and a patchwork of hay meadows below.

Sovata, about twelve kilometres off, is the notable neighbour and a good reason to come. It is a spa town built around a series of salt lakes, among them Lake Ursu, the Bear Lake, whose upper layers heat in summer sunshine and hold the warmth below, an unusual natural effect that drew visitors from the nineteenth century onward. The Praid salt mine lies not far away, where salt has been cut for centuries and visitors can walk into the mine. The region's wealth was salt, wood and sheep, and you can still see the carved wooden gateways and tidy farm buildings that came from that prosperity.

Riding in this area is relaxed and varied. The roads follow valleys and cross low ridges, with bends that open and close without drama, and long views across hay meadows toward the mountains. Surfaces are mostly decent, though patched and sometimes broken where springs or frost have done damage. Cattle and sheep use the roads freely and church bells carry across the valley in the evening. The best months are late May and June, when the flowers are thick, and the warmth of early September; winter brings snow and ice to the higher roads, and the season is short.

For food, try the Szekler dishes served in family guesthouses: stuffed cabbage, thick soups, and a sweet chimney cake called kürtőskalács baked over embers, which you will smell before you see. Eremitu is a village with a shop or two, and fuel is more reliable at Sovata, where there are stations and several cafés. Take water and a light jacket, because the hills cool fast once the sun slips behind the ridge, and take a moment to listen. In the evening, the valley sounds like it did a hundred years ago.
t.baranowka baranowka@49.1,27.0:
Podolia, the rolling country of western Ukraine between the Dniester and the Southern Bug, is a land of black soil, limestone canyons and old towns. It was a frontier between Poland, Lithuania, the Ottomans and Russia for centuries, and many of its villages carry the layers of that history, with Catholic and Orthodox churches, ruined castles and Jewish cemeteries. The label here, Baranowka, with its Polish-style spelling, gives a clue to the mix, and the ride pairing with Satanivska Dacha, a forested nature area in the region, hints at the walk and the ride on offer.

The nearby towns of Yarmolyntsi and Horodok are small market centres of the Khmelnytskyi region, with fuel, shops and cafes, and the lanes between them go through fields of wheat, sunflowers and sugar beet. Further south, the Dniester canyon cuts deep into the plateau, with the castle at Kamianets-Podilskyi standing on a rocky peninsula in the river loop, and Medzhybizh, where the Baal Shem Tov, founder of Hasidic Judaism, lived in the eighteenth century and is buried.

I have to be straight about the present. Ukraine is at war, and the whole country is subject to missile and drone attacks, military checkpoints, curfews and fuel shortages, so nobody should plan a leisure ride here without checking the latest official travel advice, and for most visitors that advice is to stay away. The western regions are far from the front line, but they are not immune. If you are reading this to plan a trip in better times, the landscape will wait.

When conditions allow, Podolia is rewarding. The roads are often rough, with potholes and patched asphalt, and the villages are slow, with horses and carts and geese on the verge. Early summer brings acacia blossom and a deep green, and autumn is warm and golden. Eat borscht, vareniki with cherries and fresh bread with salo, and be ready for hospitality that insists you eat more. The people here are generous even in hard times, and the memory of a shared table lasts longer than any monument.
t.bretcu angustia cetatea doamnei venetu@4:
There is a narrow gap in the Carpathians where Szeklerland meets the old principality of Moldavia, and the Romans, who valued narrow gaps, named their fort there Angustia, simply the narrow place. The little town of Bretcu sits on the site, in Covasna county, in a landscape of low forested mountains and wide hay meadows. The fort controlled the pass on the eastern frontier of the province of Dacia and was manned by auxiliary troops, and it forms part of the UNESCO listing for the Roman frontiers. What survives is mostly earthworks and traces of the walls, with a few explanatory signs.

The people in this region are mostly Szeklers, Hungarian speakers who have lived in the eastern Carpathians for many centuries, and the place names appear in two languages. Villages are neat, gardens are full of flowers, and carved wooden gates mark the entrances to farmyards. The region is known for its mineral springs, and bubbling water comes out of the ground in many places, and for its food. You should try kurtoskalacs, the chimney cake roasted over charcoal and rolled in sugar, which is a Szekler speciality, and a hearty stuffed cabbage, or sarmale. The market in Targu Secuiesc, the nearest real town, is a good place to find them.

The ride on this side of the Carpathians is a treat, if you pick your road. The main route over the Oituz pass towards Moldavia climbs through spruce forest on a well-maintained road with tight bends and medium gradients, and the summit is a little under nine hundred metres. This pass was the scene of fierce battles in the First World War, and the small war cemeteries by the road are a reminder of that. Traffic can be heavy with trucks, though the side roads are quiet and lovely.

Bretcu has fuel and shops, and Lemnia, just down the road, has a few more. Targu Secuiesc, fourteen kilometres away, is bigger and has everything. Weather can change quickly in the mountains, with mist and cold rain, even in summer, and winter brings snow. The best months are June to September, when the meadows are in flower and the forests are full of mushroom pickers.
t.chiheru de jos dealul pogor@46.7,25.0:
Transylvania's rolling middle country does not have an obvious centre of gravity, and Chiheru de Jos sits right in it. The village lies in Mures county, in the hills between the Gurghiu valley and the upper Mures, a region of grassy ridges, orchards, and beech and oak woods that rise to the dark mass of the Calimani and Gurghiu mountains to the east. Dealul Pogor, the Pogor hill, is the kind of local landmark that appears on large-scale maps and not on tourist ones, and I cannot tell you of any specific monument at the exact spot, so I would rather talk about the country around it.

This is a landscape of villages strung along streams, with a mix of Romanian, Hungarian and Saxon heritage, and the three have left their marks on the buildings. Small wooden or stone churches stand on hilltops, many of them fortified by the Saxons against the Ottoman and Tatar raids of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Haystacks still dot the meadows in summer, farmers use horses and carts, and the pace of life is slow. Reghin, a town not far away, is known across Europe for its violin makers, who use the resonance spruce from the surrounding mountains, and it has a long tradition of crafting instruments.

Riding here is gentle and rewarding. The minor roads climb and dip across the hills, with moderate bends, views over the valleys and a mix of surfaces that range from smooth asphalt to rough patches with potholes, and you often share the road with horse carts, tractors, dogs and geese. Traffic on the national roads can be heavy, with slow lorries, so overtaking requires patience. The best seasons are late spring, when the hills turn green and the orchards bloom, and early autumn, with warm light and golden beech forests. In winter snow and ice make the hill roads dangerous.

The nearest services are in Eremitu and Chiheru de Jos itself, with a couple of thousand people each, which means a small shop and perhaps a petrol pump, but for reliable fuel, a meal and a bed, head to Reghin or Targu Mures. Romanian village hospitality is generous, and plum brandy, ţuică, is often offered, which is best declined politely if you are riding.
t.satan vska dacha@49.2,26.2:
Ukraine's Podillia is a gently rolling country of black soil, but along its southwestern edge a line of strange ridges rises out of the fields, and Satanivska Dacha lies among them. The ridges are the Tovtry, a belt of low hills made from fossil reefs, remains of a barrier reef that grew in the warm shallow sea that covered the region some twenty million years ago, in the Miocene. The rock is limestone studded with shells and corals, and the ridge runs for hundreds of kilometres, a landscape unlike anything else in eastern Europe. The area is protected as part of the Podilski Tovtry National Nature Park.

I cannot tell you exactly what Satanivska Dacha is on the ground, but the name suggests an old country estate or hunting reserve, and the surrounding landscape is oak and hornbeam woodland, meadows, limestone outcrops and the deep, winding canyons of the Zbruch and the Dniester rivers. The Zbruch, a small river with a deep valley, formed the border between the Austrian and Russian empires in the nineteenth century, and it was here that a remarkable stone idol, a four-faced pillar called the Zbruch Idol, was found in 1848, a relic of pre-Christian Slavic belief that is now in a museum in Krakow.

The nearest town of any size is Husiatyn, on the Zbruch, a small place with an old fortress-synagogue and a ruined castle, with some fuel and food. The riding is gentle and rural, along roads that pass through villages with whitewashed cottages, orchards and sunflowers, and many surfaces are rough, with potholes and patches. Fuel stations are scattered, so top up where you can. The war in Ukraine has changed everything about travel, and conditions can vary, so check the current situation carefully before planning anything.

In peacetime, the best season is late spring, when the fields are green and the orchards in bloom, or early autumn, when the beech woods turn gold. Summers are warm and thundery. Winters are cold with deep snow.

The local food is robust and generous: borshch, varenyky dumplings with cherries or potatoes, and honey. Hospitality in village homes is legendary, and a cup of tea turns into a feast.
t.church of the resurrection of sucevita m:
Green is the colour that defines Suceviţa, and it is a green you have to see to believe. The monastery, in the Bukovina hills of northern Romania, was built at the end of the sixteenth century by the Movilă family, princes of Moldavia, and its church of the Resurrection is covered, outside as well as in, with frescoes that run in unbroken bands over every wall. Where the neighbouring monasteries of Voroneț and Moldovița are known for blue and yellow, the dominant tone here is a deep, mossy green, and the effect in the shade of the surrounding spruce is almost underwater.

The painted churches of Moldavia, a group listed by UNESCO in 1993, served a practical purpose. Most of the congregation could not read, so the walls told the Bible and the lives of the saints in pictures, and the outer paintings faced the weather on a wide overhanging roof. Suceviţa is famous for the Ladder of Virtue, a huge fresco of the soul's climb to heaven, in which a line of tiny figures ascends a ladder while demons drag the sinners off the rungs. Look for it on the north side of the church. The monastery is also fortified, with high stone walls and corner towers, because this was frontier country and the Ottomans and Poles were never far away. Nuns live here today, and visitors should dress modestly and keep voices low.

The ride to the monastery is a pleasure in itself. The valley is lined with traditional wooden houses with carved gateways, hay meadows, and slopes of spruce, and the road up from the Moldovița side crosses a forested pass with curves, short climbs and a surface that is generally good. Expect farm vehicles, horses and carts and families walking to church on Sundays. Fog and cold rain can arrive quickly even in summer, and winter brings snow.

Suceviţa is a village of about two and a half thousand, and fuel is better found in larger towns such as Rădăuți or Câmpulung Moldovenesc. The small guesthouses in the village serve home cooking, with polenta, sour cream, cheese, smoked meats and sarmale, stuffed cabbage, and the nuns' stall sells honey, icons and jam.

Go in the morning on a weekday, before the coaches arrive from Suceava.
t.la crosse@43.8,-91.2:
A rider could spend a week in La Crosse and never be bored by the view. The city lies on a flat strip of land between the Mississippi River and a line of steep, wooded bluffs, at the point where the Black and La Crosse rivers join the big river, and it feels like the middle of the Midwest folded into a valley. Grandad Bluff, a rocky headland rising almost two hundred metres above the town, gives the best look at the whole scene, with the river, the islands and Minnesota on the far side.

The surrounding country is called the Driftless Area, because the glaciers of the last ice age passed it by, leaving no layer of drift behind. Instead of flat plains, the land is cut by deep, winding valleys, known locally as coulees, with steep ridges and spring-fed streams. The result is some of the best motorcycle riding in the upper Midwest, with narrow roads that twist along creeks and climb onto the ridgetops, past dairy farms, red barns and, in the south-east, the horse-drawn buggies of Amish families. Surfaces are mostly good, though gravel appears at farm entrances and manure on the road is a fact of life.

The river road, Highway 35, is part of the Great River Road, and runs along the Mississippi past lock and dam structures, backwaters thick with herons and egrets, and small towns with brick main streets. In autumn, the bluffs light up with maple red and oak gold, and bald eagles gather along the open water in winter. The name La Crosse comes from French traders who saw the Native game played with a stick that looked like a bishop's crozier.

The city has fuel, food, motels and a lively brewing tradition, and La Crescent, across the river in Minnesota, is known for apples. Summer is humid and thunderstorms roll in quickly, while May and September are ideal. Deer are a major hazard on the back roads at dusk.
t.bicaz@46.9,26.1:
Bicaz is a town of some eight thousand people at the eastern end of the Bicaz Gorge, in the Moldavian foothills of the Carpathians, and it is known for two big things, a dam and a cement works. The dam, completed in 1960 on the Bistrița river, holds back Izvorul Muntelui, the largest reservoir in Romania by volume, a long arm of water that fills the valley and reaches far into the hills. The cement works, a concrete reminder of the communist industrial plan, still dominates one side of town. It sounds grim, but the lake is beautiful and the hills around it are green.

The real attraction is what lies to the west. Beyond Bicaz the road DN12C enters the Bicaz Gorge, or Cheile Bicazului, where limestone walls rise sheer on both sides for hundreds of metres, and the road squeezes between them beside a stream, passing through hairpins so tight that big lorries have to reverse. The gorge is narrow, damp and spectacular, with the sky reduced to a strip, and the road is lined with stalls selling wool socks, honey and cheeses. Above it, the road climbs to Lacu Roșu, the Red Lake, formed in 1837 when an earthquake sent a mountainside crashing into the valley and dammed the stream. Dead tree trunks still stand in the water.

The road connects Moldavia to Transylvania, and is used by heavy trucks, so the narrow sections can be tricky, with oncoming lorries swinging wide on the bends. Take it slowly and watch the surface, which can be wet and slippery. A quiet weekday morning is best. In summer, cool air flows out of the gorge, and in winter ice makes it hazardous.

Bicaz has fuel stations, supermarkets and small restaurants, so stock up here, because the road beyond has few services. In the villages you can try mămăligă, a polenta, with sour cream and cheese, and the sausages known as mici, grilled and served with mustard. Late spring and early autumn give the best conditions, with clear air and fewer crowds. The smell of pine and wet rock in the gorge is very strong.
t.oulu@65.0,25.5:
Oulu is the biggest city in northern Finland and sits where the Oulu River meets the Gulf of Bothnia, on land so flat that the horizon seems to go on without a bump. For centuries it was a tar port. Pine tar from the forests inland, vital for waterproofing wooden ships, was floated down the river and shipped out to Europe, and in the early nineteenth century Oulu was one of the world's largest tar exporters. When steam and steel replaced wood, the city turned to timber, then to technology, and today it is known for a big university and a strong electronics industry.

The city is a good one to wander. Cyclists are everywhere, even in winter, thanks to hundreds of kilometres of cycle paths, and there are river islands, parks and a lively market square with a handsome old market hall where you can get coffee and local pastries. A statue of a policeman, the Toripolliisi, stands on the square. The light is part of the character. In midsummer the sun barely sets, and the evenings glow a soft pink well after midnight, while in December the daylight shrinks to a few hours and the snow does the work of illuminating the streets.

For a rider, Oulu is more of a base than a destination, and the surrounding country is gentle rather than dramatic. Roads are long, straight and quiet, running through spruce, pine and bog, with wide skies and little traffic outside the city. Speed limits are low and enforced with cameras and patrols, so enjoy the scenery at the legal pace. Reindeer and elk can wander onto the road, particularly in the north and at dusk, so keep your speed down if you are riding in the evening. There are plenty of fuel stations in the city and in the neighbouring towns of Kempele and Oulunsalo, and cafés open early.

The riding season is short, from late May to early September, and weather swings from cool and drizzly to warm and bright within a day. Bring layers, and if you can, a mosquito-proof plan for any stop near water in July, since those insects have a fierce reputation. Salmon soup, a creamy local staple, is worth ordering when you stop to eat.
t.brasov@45.7,25.6:
Braşov is the tidiest of the Saxon cities of Transylvania, a medieval town of red roofs and colourful baroque façades, ringed by wooded mountains and watched over by the bare rock of Tâmpa. The German settlers who built it in the thirteenth century called it Kronstadt, and it grew rich as a trading post at the crossing of routes between the Danube plains and Central Europe. The Black Church, the largest Gothic church between Vienna and Istanbul, dominates the old centre, and got its name after a great fire in 1689 blackened the walls. It houses an enormous organ and a collection of Anatolian carpets, given by merchants who traded in the East.

The main square, the Council Square, is lined with cafes, and the old Council House stands in the middle. Nearby, Rope Street, said to be one of the narrowest streets in Europe, squeezes between the buildings to a width of little over a metre. A cable car carries you up Tâmpa, where a large white sign spells out the city's name on the hillside, and the view over the roofs and the plain is worth the ride. About 276,000 people live here, and the city has the busy air of a regional capital.

Outside town, the landscape quickly turns wild. Bran Castle, popularly known as Dracula's castle, is about thirty kilometres to the south-west, and the high cliffs of Piatra Craiului rise beyond it. The route to Moieciu and the Drumul Carului, the Cart Road, runs through a pastoral landscape of meadows, sheep farms, and scattered houses, with views of the mountain wall behind. The road is a pleasure, winding, with gentle gradients, and traffic is lighter than on the main route through Bran, though it can be busy on summer weekends. Bears are numerous in the Brașov area, and while they are shy, do not leave food outside, and keep a distance from any you see.

For fuel and services, Brașov has everything, from stations to workshops and supermarkets. Fill up before heading out, since villages in the hills have fewer stations. The food is hearty, with grilled sausages, polenta and a dessert called papanași, fried doughnuts with sour cream and jam.

Come in the afternoon, since the light on the old town is lovely, and finish with a walk through the square.
t.prairie du chien@43.1,-91.1:
Prairie du Chien lies at the spot where the Wisconsin River meets the Mississippi, and the French noticed. In June 1673, Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet, paddling down from the Wisconsin, reached the great river somewhere near here, and the settlement that grew up became a fur-trading center, one of the oldest European outposts in the upper Midwest. The name means prairie of the dog, and it is usually said to come from a Fox chief whose name meant dog.

The island in the river, St. Feriole, is where history is easiest to see. Villa Louis, a Victorian mansion built by the Dousman family, who grew rich in the fur trade, stands on the site of an earlier fort, and the grounds and house, with their carriages, wallpaper and billiard room, are beautifully kept. Nearby, the Fort Crawford Museum remembers the army post that once guarded this crossing, and the story of Dr. William Beaumont and his work on digestion is told in the medical museum. The town itself has a handsome old main street and a long river levee.

For riders, the Great River Road is the point. Wisconsin Highway 35 follows the Mississippi south and north, with bluffs rising on the east and the broad, slow river to the west, and the road has gentle curves, long views and little traffic outside summer weekends. The region is part of the Driftless Area, an unusual patch of land that missed the last glaciation, so its hills, ridges and coulees are sharp and deep, unlike the flattened country around. Eagles perch on the dead trees by the water in winter.

Prairie du Chien has fuel, supermarkets and several restaurants, with motels along the main road. It is the biggest town for a good distance, so top up here. Across the river, the Iowa bluffs hold Effigy Mounds National Monument, an ancient burial ground of animal-shaped earthworks. The best months are late September to mid-October, when the bluffs blaze with color, though May and June are green and fresh. Summer is warm and humid, with thunderstorms and occasional river flooding that can close low-lying roads. Watch for barge traffic on the water and deer on the road at dusk.
t.viroqua@43.6,-90.9:
Viroqua sits on a ridge in the Driftless country of southwestern Wisconsin, and the rolling, many-folded land around it is the point. The glaciers that flattened most of the Midwest flowed around this region, and the result is a maze of steep hills, narrow valleys and winding creeks that feels more like Appalachia than Wisconsin. Farms cling to the ridgetops, and the valleys below hold cool springs and trout streams, so every road seems to climb a crest or dive into a hollow.

The town is a pleasant surprise. A handsome Art Deco theater from the 1920s, the Temple, anchors the downtown, and the shops and cafes around the square cater to a mix of old farm families and newcomers who came for organic farming. The area is a hub of the organic movement, with a large cooperative of dairy farms nearby, and the Saturday farmers' market in the center is a delight for local cheese, bread and vegetables. Amish families, who farm with horses, live in the surrounding hills, and their buggies are a common sight on the roads, along with signs selling quilts, baked goods and furniture.

For a rider the roads are the draw. County highways wind through the coulees, with curves, short climbs and long views, and the Kickapoo River valley to the east is one of the crookedest rivers in the country, twisting back and forth through steep wooded bluffs. The Kickapoo Valley Reserve preserves land that was meant for a dam in the 1960s, an unfinished project that was eventually abandoned. Westby, a few miles away, is a Norwegian-American town where lefse and Syttende Mai celebrations keep the old traditions alive.

Viroqua has fuel, a supermarket and a number of good places to eat, and it is the best base for exploring the area. La Crosse, about forty kilometers west, is the larger city. The best season is mid-October, when the hills glow with color, though spring is lovely, with redbud and new leaf. Watch carefully for buggies, which are slow and sometimes hard to see around curves, particularly at dusk. Gravel on road shoulders and sudden fog in the valleys are other hazards.
t.brasov@45.6,25.6:
Brașov is a city built against a mountain. The wooded slope of Tâmpa rises straight from the old town, topped by a giant white sign in the style of Hollywood, and a cable car takes you to the summit for the view over red tiled roofs and the Carpathian foothills. Behind the city the high peaks of the Postăvarul and Piatra Mare ranges ring the horizon, and winter snow lies on them from late autumn.

The city was founded in the thirteenth century by Saxon settlers, who called it Kronstadt, and grew rich on trade between Transylvania, Wallachia and the Ottoman lands. Their legacy is the centre, laid out around Council Square with its baroque houses and the old Council House, and the Black Church, the largest Gothic church in southeastern Europe, named for the soot that darkened its walls after a great fire in 1689. Its organ is famous, and concerts in summer are well worth hearing. Do not miss Strada Sforii, Rope Street, one of the narrowest in Europe.

Brașov is also the starting point for some of the finest riding in Romania. An hour or two to the west lies the Transfăgărășan, the high road across the Făgăraș Mountains, which is usually closed by snow from roughly late autumn to early summer, so check the opening date before you plan. Closer by, Bran Castle, often marketed as Dracula's home, stands in the pass towards Rucăr, and the fortified church at Prejmer, a UNESCO site, shows how villagers once sheltered from raiders inside their own walls.

The city is big, with heavy traffic at rush hour and plenty of fuel on the main roads. Parking near the old town is metered but manageable, and cobbled lanes call for care in the wet. Come between June and September for the best mountain weather, but expect afternoon storms.

Eat well here: grilled meat with polenta, sour soup, and papanași, fried doughnuts with jam and cream, are all local favourites.
t.moieciu drumul carului@45.5,25.3:
Between Bran and Rucăr, the road climbs over the saddle that separates the Bucegi mountains from Piatra Craiului, through a landscape of high meadows, hay barns, scattered farms and limestone peaks. The name Drumul Carului, the cart road, recalls the old route across this pass, which has linked Transylvania and Wallachia for centuries, and archaeologists have recorded a Roman-era site here, part of the network of frontier and road posts in Dacia. Fundata, at the top, is one of the highest villages in Romania, at around 1,350 metres, and the scattered houses of Moieciu, Peștera and Șirnea spread across the hills around it.

The Bran-Rucăr corridor is one of the most beautiful areas in Romania. Piatra Craiului, a long, sharp limestone ridge, rises to the west, home to chamois, bears and rare flowers, and the Bucegi plateau, with its strange rock formations, rises to the east. In summer, shepherds take their flocks to the high pastures, and in autumn, the forests turn gold and red. The villages are known for their cheese, especially the smoked cheese wrapped in fir bark.

Bran Castle, nine kilometres away, is famous worldwide as Dracula's castle, though its connection with Vlad the Impaler is tenuous. It was a customs fortress guarding the pass, and later a royal residence of Queen Marie of Romania. It is very busy in summer, with crowds and souvenir stalls.

The road over the pass, the DN73, is a good ride, with curves and views, but it is busy with trucks and tourists, especially at weekends. The side roads into the villages are narrow, steep and sometimes unpaved, and the weather can change quickly, with fog, rain and snow. Bran has fuel, shops and accommodation, and Brașov, a larger city with a medieval centre, is about thirty kilometres north. Try the local cheeses, polenta and soups in the mountain guesthouses.
t.sarateni casa sarii@46.6,25.0:
Salt has shaped this corner of Transylvania for thousands of years. Beneath the hills of the Sovata and Praid area lies a huge salt dome, and in places it reaches the surface, creating salt cliffs, salty springs and lakes. Sărățeni, a village in the Târnava Mică valley, takes its name from the salt, and Casa Sării, the salt house, is the local name for the spot marked here. The Romans valued this salt as much as Dacian gold, and the eastern frontier of their province ran along these hills, with a fort at Sărățeni among the posts that watched the valleys and, no doubt, the salt routes.

The area is in the Székely Land, where most people speak Hungarian, and the villages have carved wooden gates, fortified churches and a strong sense of identity. Sovata, six kilometres away, is a spa town, famous for Lake Ursu, the bear lake, a heliothermal lake where the salt water is warmer at depth than at the surface, creating unusual conditions for bathing. Praid, nearby, has a salt mine open to visitors, with vast underground chambers used as a sanatorium and leisure area.

The Corund area, to the east, is known for its pottery, and the road between Sovata, Praid and Corund is lined with stalls selling ceramics, wood carvings and textiles.

For riders, the roads in the area are pleasant, with gentle curves through hills, forests and valleys, and the road from Sovata over the Bucin pass toward Gheorgheni climbs through forests to over 1,200 metres, with good views. Traffic is moderate, and surfaces are generally good, though some side roads are rough. Sovata has fuel, shops and accommodation. Roadside grills in the Székely villages turn out mici and goulash, and the bakeries sell kürtőskalács, rolled in sugar and walnuts, warm from the spit. Summer is the busiest time, so consider spring or autumn for a quieter visit.
t.village of prejmer tartlau@45.7,25.8:
In the Burzenland plain east of Brașov, the village of Prejmer, known to its Saxon founders as Tartlau, is home to one of the most remarkable buildings in Romania: a fortified church surrounded by massive circular walls, with hundreds of storage rooms built into them on several levels. The church was begun in the thirteenth century by the Teutonic Knights, who were invited into the region by the Hungarian king to defend the frontier, and later strengthened by the Saxon villagers, who built the walls to protect themselves against Ottoman and Tatar raids. It is part of the UNESCO listing of villages with fortified churches in Transylvania.

Inside the walls, the church has a Gothic interior with a beautiful winged altarpiece, and the rooms in the walls, reached by wooden stairs and galleries, were used to store food and belongings, and to shelter families during sieges. The walls were equipped with an organ of death, a battery of guns that could fire in sequence. The village itself has wide streets and colourful houses built by the Saxons, many of whom emigrated to Germany after the fall of communism, leaving the villages to new inhabitants.

The riding around Prejmer is mostly flat, with good roads across the plain and views of the Carpathian mountains rising on all sides. From Brașov, a short ride away, the good roads fan out in every direction, towards Bran Castle and Râșnov fortress, and further afield, the Transfăgărășan and Transalpina high mountain roads. Traffic can be heavy around Brașov, and horse carts and livestock are common in villages.

Prejmer, a village of around eight thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Brașov has everything else. Local cuisine includes Transylvanian dishes such as goulash, sarmale and kürtőskalács, a sweet chimney cake baked over coals, often sold at markets and fairs. Visit the fortified church early or late in the day, when the light is soft and the crowds are small.
t.church of the beheading of st john the b:
Arbore is a village in Bucovina, in the north of Romania, and its church is one of the famous painted churches of Moldavia. It was built in 1503 by Luca Arbore, a nobleman at the court of Stephen the Great, and dedicated to the Beheading of St John the Baptist. Like the other painted churches of the region, its exterior walls are covered with frescoes, applied in the sixteenth century to teach the Bible to ordinary people who could not read. Arbore's frescoes, painted around 1541, are known for their green tones, and while weather has faded the walls facing the prevailing wind, the west facade still shows scenes of the Last Judgement, saints and the Book of Genesis in remarkable detail. UNESCO lists it among the eight churches of northern Moldavia.

Unlike the larger monasteries of Voroneț, Sucevița and Moldovița, Arbore is a simple parish church, without a fortified enclosure, standing in a quiet churchyard among old trees. It is often less crowded, which gives you time to look closely at the paintings and to notice the details: the faces of the saints, the colours, and the way artists adapted the walls to their stories.

Not far away, the Codrul Secular Slătioara is one of the last old-growth forests in Romania, with fir, spruce and beech trees hundreds of years old, now protected as a nature reserve and part of the UNESCO beech forests listing. Walking among these giants, with moss and fallen trunks everywhere, is a strong contrast to the farmed landscape of the valley.

The riding in Bucovina is very rewarding. The roads between the painted churches cross wooded hills and green valleys, with some excellent passes, such as Ciumârna between Sucevița and Moldovița. Surfaces vary from smooth to badly potholed, and horse-drawn carts are common, so be alert, especially at night when they may lack lights. Arbore, with nearly seven thousand inhabitants, has basic shops and a fuel station is close by, and Rădăuți and Suceava are larger towns. Try the local sour soup, ciorbă, and papanași, fried doughnuts with sour cream and jam.
t.churches of moldavia@47.8,25.7:
Sucevița is the last and the largest of the great painted monasteries of Bucovina, and when you come down into its valley and see it for the first time, a squat fortress of white walls and towers with a church inside painted from eaves to plinth in deep greens, reds and blues, it stops you in your tracks. It was built in the 1580s and 1590s by the Movilă family, princes and churchmen of Moldavia, and its frescoes are among the best preserved of all the painted churches. UNESCO groups it with seven others as the churches of Moldavia.
