The north wall holds the most famous image: the Ladder of Virtues, a huge composition in which monks climb a ladder of thirty rungs towards heaven, angels on one side helping them up, and on the other a crowd of little black demons trying to pull them off, with some tumbling down into the open mouth of hell. It is vivid, funny and frightening at once, and it was designed to be. The north walls of most painted churches have faded in the weather, which makes Sucevița's so remarkable. Inside, every surface is painted too, and the nuns who live here keep the place immaculate.

The ride to Sucevița is part of the experience. From Moldovița, the road climbs over the Ciumârna pass, through spruce forest with tight hairpins and fine views back over the hills, before dropping down to the monastery. In the other direction it runs east through Marginea, a village famous for its black pottery, fired in a smoky kiln that gives the clay a deep, glossy black, and on to Rădăuți. The roads are mostly paved and in reasonable shape, but potholes and gravel appear without warning, and horse carts and logging trucks are regular companions.

Sucevița village has guesthouses and small shops. For fuel, head to Marginea, nine kilometres away, or Rădăuți. Bucovina is a land of good, simple food: try ciorbă rădăuțeană, a creamy chicken soup with garlic and vinegar that originated in Rădăuți, and the local sour cream and cheeses. Dress modestly to enter the monastery; women may be asked to cover their heads and legs, and there are usually wraps at the gate.
t.inlaceni cetate@46.4,25.1:
Székely Land, in the eastern part of Transylvania, is the home of a Hungarian-speaking community whose ancestors were placed here in the Middle Ages to guard the eastern frontier of the Kingdom of Hungary, and the same job had been done a thousand years earlier by the Romans. Near the village of Inlăceni, in the hills of Harghita county, stand the remains of a Roman fort, one of the eastern bastions of Dacia, facing the Carpathians and the passes beyond. The stone walls, gates and corner towers can still be traced in a meadow on a hilltop, and the setting, with forests all around and the mountains on the horizon, is one of the most beautiful of all the sites on the Dacian frontier listed by UNESCO.

The region is rich in surprises. A short ride north-east, the village of Corund is famous for its pottery, with dozens of workshops and roadside stalls selling bowls, plates and jugs painted in blue, green and brown. Further north, Praid has one of the largest salt mines in the country, which you can visit deep underground, and Sovata, a little spa town, has the Bear Lake, a salt lake whose surface warms up like a natural solar collector. Odorheiu Secuiesc, the main town of the area, has a pleasant centre and a strong Hungarian character, and signs are often bilingual.

The riding is excellent. The roads between Odorheiu Secuiesc, Corund and Praid wind through hills and forests with good surfaces and moderate traffic, and further east, the road over the Harghita mountains towards Miercurea Ciuc climbs through dense spruce forests to a high pass. To the west, the road to Sighișoara descends through rolling countryside of Saxon villages and fortified churches. Watch out for horse carts, especially in the villages, and for bears, which are common in the forests of Harghita and occasionally cross the road at dusk.

Corund and Odorheiu Secuiesc have fuel, shops and restaurants. Try kürtőskalács, the chimney cake, a sweet bread rolled on a spit and baked over coals, then coated with sugar or walnuts, and the hearty Székely dishes, such as goulash soup and stuffed cabbage. Guesthouses are plentiful and welcoming, and many have their own pálinka to offer.
t.baile homorod cekend@46.4,25.5:
Deep in the forests of Harghita county, in the heart of the Székely Land, the small spa of Băile Homorod sits in a valley among spruce and beech, with wooden villas, mineral springs and the smell of resin in the air. The springs here produce borvíz, naturally carbonated mineral water, which the Székely people drink as their everyday water and believe has healing powers. Cekend is the name attached to a nearby hill site on the eastern line of Roman Dacia's frontier, one of hundreds of components listed together as a World Heritage Site in 2024.

The Székely Land is a Hungarian speaking region in the east of Transylvania, with its own traditions, carved wooden gates, fortified churches and folk costumes. The village of Dârjiu, nearby, has a fortified church with a medieval mural cycle, part of the World Heritage listing of Villages with Fortified Churches in Transylvania. Odorheiu Secuiesc, Székelyudvarhely in Hungarian, is the main town of the area.

The landscape is mountainous and forested, with the Harghita mountains, volcanic in origin, rising to the east. Bears are common in these forests, and you should take care when walking. The air is cool even in summer, and winters are cold and snowy.

The riding here is excellent: winding roads through forests and over passes, with good surfaces on the main roads and rougher ones on the minor roads. The road from Odorheiu Secuiesc to Miercurea Ciuc over the Harghita mountains is a beautiful ride, and the routes to Lake Sfânta Ana, a volcanic crater lake, are worth the detour. Watch for horse carts, livestock and bears.

The spa had its heyday in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when families from the towns of Transylvania came for weeks at a time to drink the waters, bathe and walk in the woods. Some of the old villas, with carved wooden balconies, still stand, and several springs are open to anyone with a bottle; locals fill up jerrycans and swear by the taste, which is sharp, fizzy and faintly of iron. Vlăhița, five kilometres away, is the closest place for petrol, and Odorheiu Secuiesc has more. Try kürtőskalács, chimney cake, the Székely sweet bread baked on a spit, and the local goulash and pálinka.
t.rucar scarisoara@45.4,25.2:
Rucăr sits right where the Dâmbovița comes out of the mountains, a long village of wooden gates and tin roofs strung along the valley floor at the southern foot of the Rucăr–Bran corridor. Behind it the land climbs fast: Piatra Craiului's limestone ridge to the north-west, the rounded bulk of Leaota and the Bucegi to the east, and between them the saddle that has carried traffic between Wallachia and Transylvania for as long as anyone has bothered to write things down.

That saddle is the reason to be here. The DN73 leaves Rucăr and climbs in a series of open, well-cambered bends towards Podu Dâmboviței and the high pastures around Fundata, then drops to Bran and its famous, overmarketed castle. It is one of the friendlier mountain roads in Romania: the surface is decent, the corners are readable, and the views across hay meadows dotted with shepherds' huts are worth slowing for. The catch is traffic. Trucks use it, and so does half of Bucharest on a summer weekend, so the early morning belongs to you and the afternoon to everyone else. In wet weather watch for mud and gravel washed out of farm tracks.

People have been guarding this gap for two thousand years. The Romans held a fort near Rucăr on their frontier line through Muntenia, and in the Middle Ages the route was a customs road, with merchants from Brașov paying their dues at Bran on the way down to the Wallachian markets. Câmpulung, a short ride south, was the first seat of the Wallachian princes, and its old princely church is worth the detour if you have the energy.

Just upstream, the Dâmbovița and its tributaries have cut narrow limestone gorges, the Cheile Dâmbovicioarei among them, where the road squeezes between grey walls and the air turns cool and damp even in August. Look up and you may see choughs or a buzzard working the thermals; look down and the river is clear enough to count stones. Bears live in these forests too, so do not leave food on the bike overnight.

Rucăr itself is big enough for fuel, a small shop and a plate of something hearty, usually with polenta and sour cream on the side. Dragoslavele, a few minutes down the valley, has more of the same. Fill the tank here before you climb; the next comfortable stop is on the far side of the pass.
t.odorheiu secuiesc piatra cotofana@46.3,2:
Odorheiu Secuiesc is a town that answers to two names, and if you ask for directions you will probably hear the Hungarian one, Székelyudvarhely. This is the heart of Székely Land, the Hungarian-speaking corner of eastern Transylvania, and the signs, the church spires and the way people greet you all make that plain within a minute of arriving. Piatra Coțofană, the Magpie Stone, is one of the rocky heights on the hills around the town, a few kilometres out among pasture and beech woods.

The town sits in the valley of the Târnava Mare, which starts its long westward journey not far away in the Harghita mountains. To the east rise the volcanic Harghita heights, wooded and soft-shouldered; to the west the land rolls out in long ridges towards the Saxon villages and Sighișoara. Riding here is less about drama than rhythm: county roads that climb over one ridge, drop into a village, cross a stream and climb again, with hay meadows on both sides and horse carts as the main traffic hazard. Surfaces vary from fresh tarmac to patched and potholed, sometimes on the same kilometre, so keep your eyes up.

The Székelys were frontier guards for the medieval Hungarian kingdom, free men who paid for their privileges with military service, and their pride in that history is everywhere. You will see carved wooden Székely gates, big roofed portals with dovecotes along the top, in front of farmyards in nearly every village. In town there is a small park of busts of Hungarian notables, a handsome baroque Catholic church on the main square, and bakeries selling kürtőskalács, the chimney cake wound around a spit and rolled in sugar or walnuts.

One of the rides from here heads out to Viscri, the fortified Saxon village that became famous when King Charles bought a house there, and the change in landscape as you cross from Székely to Saxon country is worth noticing: different churches, different house shapes, a different language on the gravestones.

Practically, Odorheiu Secuiesc is a proper town with fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and places to sleep, so it makes a relaxed base. The hills around Piatra Coțofană are good for a short walk and a look back over the roofs. Evenings get cool even in summer at this height, so keep a layer handy.
t.felschtin felschtin@49.3,26.7:
Felshtin is a name that has almost disappeared from maps. The Yiddish name belongs to a small town in Podolia, in western Ukraine, now called Hvardiiske, where for generations Jews and Ukrainians lived side by side among the orchards and rolling fields. The Jewish community lived by trade and craft, with a synagogue, a market square and a cemetery on the edge of town. In February 1919, during the chaos of the civil war, the town was attacked, and hundreds of its Jewish residents were murdered in one of the worst pogroms of that period. Later the community was destroyed completely in the Second World War.

What remains is mostly the cemetery, with old tombstones carved in Hebrew with symbols such as hands, lions, and trees, many of them leaning, broken or covered in moss. Hunting for the stones is a quiet and sombre experience, and visitors who come are asked to treat the place with respect, to keep to the paths and not to disturb the stones. Baranowka, mentioned in our label, is a neighbouring Jewish heritage site in the same district of Khmelnytskyi province.

I should be honest about the practical side. Ukraine is at war, and although this western region is far from the front line, there are air-raid alerts, restrictions on movement, military checkpoints and fuel shortages from time to time, and travel advice from most governments is to avoid non-essential travel. If you are thinking of visiting, check the current situation carefully, and do not plan a route without up-to-date local information. In peaceful times, the roads in Podolia are mixed, with decent main routes and rough side roads, and the countryside is gentle and pretty, with fields of sunflowers, wheat and maize.

The nearest town is Yarmolyntsi, around nineteen kilometres away, with shops and a market, and Khmelnytskyi city is larger. Podolia is also home to the Dniester canyon and the fortress of Kamianets-Podilskyi, which are among the most impressive sights in the country and, in better times, are well worth a visit. If you want to learn about the Jewish history of the region, local museums and researchers in Khmelnytskyi are the best source.
t.church of st george of the former vorone:
Voroneț is known as the Sistine Chapel of the East, and it earned the name with a colour. The little church of St George, built in 1488 by Stephen the Great, prince of Moldavia, is covered inside and out with frescoes, and the outside, especially, glows with a deep blue that has never been exactly replicated and is now called Voroneț blue. The west wall carries a vast Last Judgment, added in 1547, in which rivers of fire pull the damned toward the pit while saints, angels and a procession of animals look on. Legend says that Stephen built the church in three months, three weeks and three days after a victory over the Ottomans.

It is one of the painted churches of Bukovina, in northern Moldavia, which UNESCO listed in 1993. Others in the group are Humor, Moldovița, Suceviţa and Arbore, and they are all different, with their own colours and stories. The paintings were meant to be read by people who could not read, and the exteriors are full of saints, scenes from the Bible and sieges, set under wide overhanging eaves that protect them from the rain. The church sits in a small village in a green valley, with the nuns' dwellings next door, and is run today as a convent.

For a rider, Bucovina is a joy. The roads around Gura Humorului, the nearest town, wind through forested hills and valleys with well-kept villages, wooden houses and haystacks, and they climb to passes such as Mestecăniş, at about a thousand metres, with open views and a good surface. Traffic is moderate, though lorries and horse-drawn carts appear at times, and the weather can change quickly in the mountains. May to June, when the meadows are in flower, and September, when the beech woods turn gold, are the best months. Not far away, the Slătioara primeval forest is one of the oldest and best-preserved stands of beech in the Carpathians.

Gura Humorului, three kilometres away, has fuel stations, restaurants and plenty of guesthouses, and Bucovina is known for hospitality, with homemade food that includes sarmale, cabbage rolls, and cornmeal mush with sour cream. Women are asked to cover their heads and legs at the monastery, and men to wear long trousers; photography inside is restricted, so ask first.
t.katerinowka katerinowka@49.6,26.8:
Katerinowka is a village in the Khmelnytskyi region of western Ukraine, in the rolling farmland of Podolia, and on the map it is mainly a point on a quiet back road between larger settlements. The coordinates fall roughly between Narkevychi and Krasyliv, with the regional centre of Khmelnytskyi a little over twenty kilometres further on. I do not know a specific monument at this spot, so I will describe the land rather than invent one.

Podolia is a plateau cut by river valleys and gullies, with deep black soil that has made the region a breadbasket for centuries. Fields of wheat, sunflowers and sugar beet roll to the horizon, divided by shelter belts of poplar and acacia. Villages tend to be long, strung along a single street, with whitewashed houses, painted window frames and gardens full of sunflowers and cabbages. In summer the air smells of hay and warm earth; in late September the combine harvesters throw up clouds of dust that glow orange in the evening.

Riding conditions in rural Ukraine have always demanded attention. Surfaces can change abruptly from decent asphalt to broken patches or gravel, and potholes appear at the worst places, usually in a bend or at the bottom of a dip. Carts, tractors and livestock share the roads, and in villages the speed limits are best treated as generous. The nearest towns, Krasyliv with almost twenty thousand people and Khmelnytskyi with nearly four hundred thousand, have fuel and food, while the villages in between mostly do not.

An honest word about the present: because of the war in Ukraine, travel here depends on the current security situation, official advice and local conditions, and anyone planning to ride should check them carefully and not rely on any older description of the roads. The region has a long history of mixed communities, Polish, Ukrainian and Jewish, and old manor parks, wooden churches and ruined fortifications are scattered across the countryside. In peaceful times this is a superb place for slow, unhurried touring, and the villages have a warmth that visitors remember.
t.codrul secular slatioara@47.4,25.6:
Slătioara is old-growth forest of the kind that Europe has mostly lost. The reserve, tucked into the slopes of the Rarău and Giumalău ranges above the Moldova valley, protects beech, fir and spruce that have never been seriously logged, and it is part of the Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians that UNESCO recognised. Walk under the canopy and you notice the scale first: trunks as thick as a doorway, fallen giants furred with moss, and a dim green light even at noon.

Getting here is half the pleasure. From Câmpulung Moldovenesc, a handsome town of about twenty thousand where you will find fuel and plenty of food, the road runs along the Moldova valley, past timber yards and houses with carved gables. Stulpicani and Crucea are the nearest villages, both small, and Crucea has a mining past. Forest tracks near the reserve itself can be rough, so check the surface before you commit with a loaded bike. The tarmac approaches are generally fine, with long gentle bends and the smell of resin and wood smoke.

The Bucovina region is famous for its painted monasteries to the north, and this forest is their natural counterpart: the trees that supplied the timber, the shingles and the carved crosses for centuries of mountain life. Wildlife is part of the story, too. Brown bears, lynx and wolves live in these woods, and while you are very unlikely to see one, you should keep food packed away and not wander off at dusk. Capercaillie and other shy birds still use the old stands.

Late spring through autumn is the season. In May the beech leaves are an almost luminous green, in October the whole slope turns copper and gold, and by December snow can make the higher forest tracks impassable. Rain is frequent in the Carpathians, so bring a jacket even on a bright morning. A quiet hour here makes the later ride to the painted church at Pătrăuți feel like a journey through a continuous story of faith and forest.
t.church of the holy rood of patrauti@47.7:
In 1487 Stephen the Great of Moldavia had a small church built at Pătrăuți, dedicated to the Holy Rood, and it still stands, among the earliest of his many foundations and today part of the UNESCO listing of Moldavian churches. It is a modest building, whitewashed and low, with a steep roof, and it stands in a village on the edge of Suceava county, a stone's throw from Dărmănești. The scale surprises people who come expecting a cathedral, and then the frescoes inside bring them up short.

The story behind it is a good one. Stephen won an extraordinary run of battles against the Ottomans and the Poles and, so the tradition goes, built a church after each major victory. Whether or not every church fits that neat pattern, this one belongs to the same period of ambition, when Moldavia was a small country holding a large power at bay. Inside, the painted walls show saints in a warm, remarkable palette, and the church is a fine early example of Moldavian painting.

The road in is easy. You are close to Suceava, where fuel and food are plentiful, and Pătrăuți and Dărmănești are both small towns of four to six thousand people with basic shops and stations. Roads here are flat to gently rolling, through farmland and plum orchards, and the traffic is a mix of cars, tractors and horse carts. Nothing technical, but a pleasant warm-up for the bends of the Bucovina hills.

Visit in good light, ideally mid-morning, and do check ahead for opening hours, which can be limited. Dress respectfully, since this is a working church, with covered shoulders and no shorts. Not far to the north is Dragomirna monastery at Mitocu Dragomirnei, founded in the early seventeenth century and known for its tall, slender church, and the two stops together make a fine morning. Autumn light on the whitewash is superb, and the farmland smells of apples and woodsmoke.
t.church of st george of suceava@47.7,26.3:
Suceava is the old capital of Moldavia, and the church of St George sits at its edge, a short ride from the ring of newer apartment blocks that now surround the medieval centre. It was built in the early sixteenth century under Bogdan III, son of Stephen the Great, and it belongs to the small family of Moldavian churches that UNESCO lists together. The family resemblance is easy to see once you have visited two or three: steep roofs, a short tower over the nave, buttresses, and walls that were once painted inside and out in blue, red and ochre.

Here the exterior frescoes have weathered badly, so do not expect the glowing outdoor Last Judgement you get at Voroneț. What the church has instead is a living function. The relics of Saint John the New, a merchant martyred in Cetatea Albă and venerated as the patron of Suceava, rest inside, and in early summer the pilgrimage around his feast fills the lanes with people carrying candles and flowers. If you arrive on an ordinary weekday the place is quiet, with an old woman selling candles and a priest crossing the yard.

The riding in this corner of Bucovina is gentle and slightly absent-minded. Roads out of Suceava toward Scheia and Patrăuți are two-lane asphalt, patched, and prone to potholes where trucks have braked for years. Villages run into one another, with carved wooden gates, geese at the verge and horse carts that appear without warning, so the ride is more about speed discipline than about leaning. Dogs are an issue too. Keep a finger on the brake near farm entrances.

For practical matters, Suceava is a proper city of over a hundred thousand people, with fuel stations on every approach road, supermarkets, and cafés around the pedestrian centre. Scheia, only four kilometres away, is large enough to have fuel as well. Dress modestly if you want to step inside, with covered shoulders and knees, and a headscarf is expected for women. Photography in the nave is normally frowned on, so ask first. Come in the late afternoon when the stone turns warm and the traffic dies down, and plan the stop for the church and a coffee rather than for a long ride.
t.nyzhniy verbizh tserkva of the nativity:
The wooden church of Nyzhniy Verbizh stands in the foothills of the Carpathians, in the Pokuttya region of western Ukraine, close to the Prut river and the old town of Kolomyia. It is one of the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region listed by UNESCO in 2013, a group of sixteen churches in Ukraine and Poland that show how the Orthodox and Greek Catholic communities of the mountains developed a tradition of building in timber that mixed Byzantine plans with local carpentry. Like others in the group, this one has a cross-shaped plan with tiered roofs and a small tower, and is raised from squared logs with shingles on the roofs, in a form that dates from the early 1800s.

Inside, a wooden iconostasis, painted with saints and gilded flowers, divides the sanctuary from the nave, and the walls are often decorated with folk-style paintings. The surrounding villages belong to the Hutsuls and Pokuttya Ukrainians, mountain people with strong traditions of woodcarving, embroidery, painted Easter eggs and music. Kolomyia, a few kilometres away, has a museum of pysanky, the decorated eggs, housed in a building shaped like a giant egg, which is a surprising and charming landmark.

Riding here has an old-world charm. The roads follow river valleys and cross low ridges, with orchards and cornfields and the dark line of the Carpathians on the horizon. Surfaces vary a lot, with fine sections and others broken by frost and heavy lorries, and you need to watch for potholes, horse carts and unmarked junctions. Spring is wet and green, summer is warm, and the colours of autumn on the beech forests of the mountains are spectacular. Winter is cold and snowy.

I should add that travel in Ukraine depends entirely on the security situation, which has been very unstable, and anyone considering a trip needs to follow current official advice rather than any guidebook. This text is about the place, not a recommendation to go.

In normal times, fuel is no problem in Kolomyia, a town of about sixty thousand, and the main road across the region has stations. Village shops sell bread, cheese and sweet pastries, and a bowl of borscht or a plate of banosh, a creamy cornmeal dish with cheese and bacon, is the thing to look for in a mountain cafe. The church is still used for worship, so cover your shoulders and speak softly.
t.campulung jidova 2@45.2,25.0:
Jidova is a quiet edge of Câmpulung with an unusually grand past. On a low rise at the town's edge, in the foothills of the Southern Carpathians, the Romans built a fort, Jidava, in the early second century AD, as part of a line of defences, the Limes Transalutanus, which ran along the edge of the mountains to protect the province of Dacia from the peoples to the east. The fort was of earth and later stone, with a garrison of auxiliary soldiers, and it covered a rectangular platform that archaeologists have traced and partly excavated. The ride list calls the site Jidova 2, a reference to a second archaeological area, and the remains are modest, with stone foundations in the grass.

Câmpulung itself has a good claim to be the first capital of Wallachia. Local tradition holds that the legendary prince Radu Negru, Black Rudolph, descended from Transylvania here in the thirteenth century and founded the principality, and the town has an old church, the Negru Vodă monastery, said to be his. Whatever the truth of the legend, the town was an early seat of power in the region, and it remained a significant place on the route between Wallachia and Transylvania.

That route is the reason a rider comes. From Câmpulung, the road climbs northwest through Rucăr to the Bran Pass, a mountain gap that links Wallachia with the Braşov region, with views of the Piatra Craiului ridge and fine bends through beech and spruce forest. Traffic can be heavy with lorries, especially in summer, and the surface is mixed, but the scenery is memorable. In spring, the meadows are dotted with flowers and the hills are green, while in autumn, the beeches turn gold and orange. Winter brings snow and ice, so check conditions. Fog and rain can come quickly in the mountains.

Câmpulung has a population of around thirty thousand, so fuel, supermarkets and restaurants are plentiful, and the smaller places nearby, such as Schitu-Goleşti and Godeni, are quieter. A good stop is a restaurant for ciorbă de burtă, a tripe soup, and papanași, a doughnut with sour cream and jam.

Remember that the fort lies on private and farm land in places, so ask before crossing fields.
t.la crosse@43.8,-91.3:
Grandad Bluff gives La Crosse its postcard view: a limestone headland rising about 150 metres over the city, from which the whole valley lies open, the Mississippi sliding past in several braided channels, the wooded bluffs of Minnesota on the far side, and the Wisconsin river towns lining the shore. On a clear autumn day the colour is extraordinary, the oaks and maples turning red and gold along miles of ridgeline. A road climbs to the top, and the view is free.

The city of about fifty thousand sits in the Driftless Area, an unusual pocket of the Upper Midwest that the glaciers missed, so the land is carved into steep ridges and deep valleys, called coulees, instead of the flat plain that surrounds it. Rivers here run clear and cold, and the country is thick with dairy farms, apple orchards and small towns. The Mississippi itself is wide and slow, with locks, backwaters and islands full of herons, eagles and pelicans in the migration season. Barges push long tows of grain and coal past the city.

La Crosse is best known for beer, historically, and for a lively university and a riverside park with a statue of Hiawatha. The name comes from the game the French voyageurs saw Native Americans playing on the prairie, which they called la crosse. The city's old breweries made it a hub of German-American culture, and bratwurst and cheese curds are still on every menu. A walk along the levee, with the barges passing and the railway bridge overhead, is a pleasant stroll after a long day.

For the Great River Road, which follows the Mississippi from its source in Minnesota to the Gulf, La Crosse marks a turning point, with the road south running through some of the loveliest scenery on the route. State Highway 35 hugs the Wisconsin shore, with long runs beside the river, wooded bluffs and little towns, and the bends are gentle and the traffic light. Surface is good and speeds are modest, so it suits an easy, scenic pace. Watch for deer at dawn and dusk, and for sudden fog off the river in cool mornings.

Fuel, food and rooms are plentiful, and the city has everything a rider might need. In spring, high water can close low-lying sections of road, and in winter ice makes the bluffs treacherous, so the season for riding is late spring through October.
t.dubuque@42.5,-90.7:
Dubuque is an old river city built on a limestone bluff above the Mississippi, in the north-east corner of Iowa, where the state meets Illinois and Wisconsin. About fifty-nine thousand people live here, and the town's history goes back to 1788, when a French-Canadian trader named Julien Dubuque, with the permission of the Meskwaki people who lived here, began mining the lead that lay close to the surface. He died in 1810, and his grave, a stone tower above the river at a site called Mines of Spain, is now a state recreation area with hiking trails and views over the water.

The town grew rich in the nineteenth century on lead, lumber and river trade, and the old buildings tell the tale, with handsome brick warehouses, steepled churches and big Victorian houses on the hillside. The Fenelon Place Elevator, a tiny cable car that climbs a steep bluff for one of the shortest and steepest scenic railways in the world, has carried passengers since 1882, and the ride at sunset, with the river spread out below, is one of the pleasures of the town. The National Mississippi River Museum and Aquarium, down on the waterfront, explains the river's ecology and history well.

The Great River Road runs through Dubuque, following the river along the bluffs, and the stretch north toward Guttenberg and Prairie du Chien is among the most beautiful in the Midwest. The river here is wide and slow, with islands, backwaters and limestone cliffs, and bald eagles winter in large numbers near the locks and dams, with the best viewing from November to February. The roads are well surfaced, with gentle curves and low traffic, and the speed limits are modest. In autumn the bluffs blaze with maple and oak.

Fuel and food are plentiful in Dubuque, and there are many local restaurants serving pork tenderloin sandwiches, a Midwestern favourite, and good beer. Cross the bridge to East Dubuque in Illinois for a different view of the river. Summer is hot and humid, with thunderstorms, so spring and early autumn are the best seasons. Come at the end of the day, when the barges slide past in the dusk and the sound of the river drifts up the bluff.
t.bicaz gorge@46.8,25.8:
The Bicaz Gorge is a crack in the Carpathians, and the road goes straight through it. For several kilometres the limestone walls of the Hășmaș mountains close in on both sides, rising some three hundred metres in places, so narrow that the road and the stream beside it share the floor and the sky shrinks to a ribbon. Bends are tight, the walls overhang, and the light changes from gold to deep shadow as you go. It is one of the great short rides of Eastern Europe, and it ends too soon.

The road, the DN12C, links the Transylvanian side at Gheorgheni with Moldavia, and it follows a route that has been used for centuries. The river that carved the gorge is the Bicaz, and the rock formations carry names like the Altar Stone and the Lonely Rock. At the narrowest part, rows of stalls selling wool socks, honey, cheese, jams and carved wooden trinkets crowd the roadside in summer, which narrows the carriageway even more. In the middle of the day coaches and trucks come through, and meeting one on a blind bend is a tense moment, so take it slowly and hold your line.

A short way upstream, the Red Lake, or Lacul Roșu, is worth a detour. It was created in 1837 when a landslide dammed a valley, and dead tree trunks still rise from the water, which gives the lake a haunting look in morning mist. The surrounding forests are home to bears, deer and wolves, and the limestone cliffs support rare plants and birds of prey. The air smells of spruce and wet rock.

The best time to ride is early on a weekday morning, when traffic is light and the shadows give the walls a dramatic look, or in autumn when the forests glow. In rain the surface can be slick, and falling rocks are possible, so watch the verges. The village of Bicaz-Chei at the western end has a few shops and guesthouses, but for proper fuel it is best to fill up in Bicaz town on the Moldavian side or in Gheorgheni to the west before you enter.

Come out the far end into the open valley, and you will feel the space as if you had held your breath.
t.elizabeth@42.3,-90.2:
Elizabeth is a small village in the north-west corner of Illinois, and it sits in country that the last ice sheet missed. This is the Driftless Area, a patch of the Upper Midwest that the glaciers flowed around, which is why it is hilly, wooded and cut by steep valleys, while most of Illinois is as flat as a table. The roads here rise and fall like a ship in a swell, and the farms are laid out along ridges and valleys in contour-following strips, with red barns, limestone outcrops and woodland on every slope.

The village has a quiet history, and one dramatic episode. In 1832, during the Black Hawk War, a party of Sauk warriors attacked a small fort on the Apple River here, and the defenders, mostly local settlers and miners, held them off. The fort has been rebuilt as a state historic site, and it is worth a short stop for the story of how people lived on this frontier. The reason they were here at all was lead, which was mined in huge quantities in this district in the early nineteenth century and shipped down the Mississippi from the river port at Galena.

For a rider, this is among the best country in the Midwest. The state highways and county roads twist through the hills in long, flowing bends, with good surfaces, light traffic and views across wooded valleys that, in October, are red, orange and gold. The Mississippi is a short ride to the west, with bluffs, backwaters and the great river itself, and the Great River Road follows it for much of its length. Wind and weather can be sharp in winter, but from May to October the riding is superb. Watch for deer at dawn and dusk, and for farm traffic, particularly in the harvest.

Galena, about twenty kilometres away, is the town to visit, with its beautifully preserved nineteenth-century streets and a past as the home of Ulysses Grant. Elizabeth itself has a handful of places to eat and a small shop, and fuel is available in the larger villages nearby, though you should not push your luck on Sunday evenings. Bring a layer for the morning and check the weather in the autumn, when the first frosts arrive.
t.hanover@42.3,-90.3:
Hanover is a village of a few hundred people where the Apple River slips past low limestone bluffs on its way to the Mississippi, and the whole setting has a slow, old-fashioned charm. The river was once harnessed to run a mill, and the old mill dam and the stone buildings that went with it are still a feature of the village, with the water tumbling over the weir in a pleasant, rushing sound. A few small shops, an old stone church and a handful of houses make up the centre.

The district is part of the Driftless Area, and the hills around Hanover are among the steepest in Illinois. The Mississippi is only a few kilometres to the west, and beyond it lies Iowa, with the town of Bellevue on the other bank. At this latitude the river is wide and slow, with islands, backwaters and a series of locks and dams that make it navigable for barges. Bald eagles winter on the river, gathering near the open water below the dams, and from December to February there are good places to watch them. In spring and autumn, the river is a major flyway, and huge flocks of ducks and geese pass through.

Riding here is a matter of following the water. The road along the river runs under limestone bluffs and past farms, with long, easy bends, mostly good surface and sections where the bluffs rise straight above the road. It then climbs out of the valley onto the ridge in a series of bends, with views over the river from the top. Traffic is generally light, though motorcyclists and cyclists flock to this stretch of the Great River Road on summer weekends, and the occasional tourist in a slow car can hold things up. Look out for gravel, particularly after heavy rain.

For fuel and food, Bellevue and Savanna, each a short ride away, have the basics, and Maquoketa, in Iowa, is a larger town with more services. Hanover has little, so plan accordingly, and carry some food and water on a hot day. Autumn is the pick of the year, with the maples and oaks turning on the bluffs, but the first half of June, when the corn is high and the weather is warm, is a good second.
t.gqeberha@-34.0,25.6:
Gqeberha is the name that Port Elizabeth took in 2021, an isiXhosa word usually linked to the Gqeberha River, the stream that runs into Algoa Bay. The change still divides opinion, and you will hear both names on the street, but the city that carries them is the same big, breezy, workmanlike place on the Eastern Cape coast. It forms the heart of the Nelson Mandela Bay metropolitan area, with a car industry that has employed generations, a port, and a waterfront of long pale beaches that seem to go on forever.

For riders on Route 62, it is the far end of one of the great long-distance roads in South Africa. The route runs inland from Cape Town through the Little Karoo, a dry valley of red hills and fruit farms between two mountain ranges, passing Montagu, Barrydale, Ladismith and Oudtshoorn, then crosses the Langkloof and drops to the coast. Along the way are ostrich farms, roadside stalls selling dried fruit and rusks, and the famous pub at Ronnie's Sex Shop, a bar in the middle of nowhere that has built a legend on a hand-painted sign. The distance is about eight hundred and fifty kilometers, so most people take two or three days.

The riding is varied and mostly relaxed. There are long straight stretches in the Karoo with views that stretch to the horizon, and sections through mountain passes, such as the Tradouw and Meiringspoort, with tight, sweeping bends and sheer cliffs. The surface is generally good, and traffic is moderate outside school holidays. Summer is hot, with temperatures that can reach above forty degrees inland, while winter brings cold mornings and occasional snow on the high peaks. Wind on the coast can be fierce.

Gqeberha has every service a rider needs. Fuel stations, motorcycle dealers and mechanics are plentiful, and the city has a good restaurant scene, with seafood and braai well represented. The Donkin Reserve, a hilltop park with a lighthouse and a pyramid, gives a view over the harbor and makes a pleasant place to sit after a long ride.

Before heading home, it is worth a short run to Addo Elephant National Park, about an hour north, where herds of elephants cross the road on a regular basis. Keep your distance and your engine quiet.
t.port elizabeth@-34.0,25.6:
Port Elizabeth was founded in 1820 as a landing place for British settlers, who came by sea to Algoa Bay in a scheme to strengthen the eastern frontier of the Cape Colony. Sir Rufane Donkin, the acting governor, named the settlement after his late wife, Elizabeth, and built a stone pyramid on a hill in her memory, which still stands in the park that bears his name. The city has been renamed Gqeberha officially, but the old name persists on road signs and in daily speech, and its history is tied to the nineteenth-century wool trade and later to the car industry.

The coast to the west is the other reason to be here. The Garden Route Coast begins with Jeffreys Bay, about seventy kilometers along the N2, a surf town that is home to one of the longest and best right-hand waves in the world, and the competitions held there draw pros from everywhere. Beyond it lie small fishing villages and long, empty beaches, then the forest and gorges of the Tsitsikamma coast. The N2 is fast and well kept, but the older roads off it, especially along the sea, give more variety and the chance to see whales and dolphins from the cliffs.

For riders, the season matters. The Eastern Cape has a mild climate, and the best months are from March to May and September to November, when it is warm and dry. Summer is busy and hot, and sea fog and strong south-westerly winds can make the coast cold and damp in winter. The traffic on the N2 near the city is heavy, with trucks and fast cars, so it is better to leave early in the morning.

Everything is easy here. The city has fuel stations on almost every corner, dealerships and good repair shops, and the beachfront at Humewood has cafes, seafood restaurants and a long promenade. The Fort Frederick, a small stone fort from 1799, stands near the harbor and is one of the oldest buildings in the area.

If you are heading west toward the Garden Route, fill up here, since the road between Humansdorp and Storms River has fewer stations than you might expect.
t.qachas nek@-30.1,28.7:
Qacha's Nek is a border town in the far southeast of Lesotho, perched on a ridge at the top of a pass that the town takes its name from, with a sheer drop on one side and a view across a sea of ridges on the other. It is a remote place by any standard, and the border post, leads over the pass to the South African town of Matatiele, a short ride away. About twenty-five thousand people live in the district, and the town itself is a modest cluster of shops, government offices and guesthouses.

The ride in is a long climb through mountain country, on roads that are mostly paved and sometimes broken. The route from the north runs through high valleys with wide views, and the final approach to the town winds up the escarpment in a series of bends with fine views. The road toward Sehlabathebe is a different matter: it is gravel and rough, and leads to a remote national park, so it is a ride for experienced riders on suitable bikes. Weather can be cold, wet and misty, and in winter snow can close roads. Livestock, minibus taxis and the odd rock on the road all demand attention.

The town has a history as a frontier. The pass was long used by herders and traders moving between Lesotho and the Eastern Cape, and the border was drawn along the Drakensberg ridge in the nineteenth century when the territory became a British protectorate. Remote mountain communities here have preserved much of the traditional Basotho way of life, including the herding of cattle and sheep and the building of round stone huts with thatched roofs. The Sehlabathebe National Park, southeast of town, is a UNESCO World Heritage extension for its natural and cultural value, with rock art and a lake in a high, wild plateau.

Nature is rugged and cold. The highlands are covered in grass and shrub, with rocky outcrops and the occasional stand of trees, and the rivers are clear and cold. Rare wildlife includes the bearded vulture and the Maloti minnow, a fish found only in these mountain streams, and the sky is huge. In winter, the peaks wear a mantle of snow.

You can buy fuel and food in town, which is useful, as supplies thin out quickly in the mountains. Bring passport, vehicle papers and insurance, carry warm clothes, and allow extra time for border formalities and for the road.
t.piatra neamt@46.9,26.4:
Piatra Neamț is a proper Moldavian town of around a hundred thousand people sitting in a bowl of forested hills, and it makes a very good place to start a ride into the Eastern Carpathians. The Bistrița river runs just to the south, the Ceahlău massif stands on the western horizon, and on a clear morning the whole thing looks like a model of itself. Fuel, supermarkets, cash machines and big breakfasts are all easy here, so do whatever errands you have before you go.

The old centre has more history than most visitors expect. Stephen the Great, the fifteenth-century prince of Moldavia who fought off Ottoman armies for decades and founded dozens of churches, built a princely court here, and a tower from that period still stands near the main square, together with a church of his that has survived for centuries. The town's museums also hold material from the Cucuteni culture, a Neolithic people who painted beautiful spiral-patterned pottery in this region some six thousand years ago. If you have an hour, the pottery is worth seeing before you head out.

The ride begins by climbing out along the river, past the huge artificial Bicaz lake, which was created in the middle of the last century by a concrete dam and now fills a long mountain valley with a green-grey sheet of water. The road follows its shore for many kilometres with lots of gentle bends, small villages, roadside stalls selling honey and smoked cheese, and views over to forested slopes. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with lorries mixed in, so patience and a steady pace work better than hurrying.

The scenery gets dramatic as you push on toward Bicaz Gorge, where the valley narrows and limestone walls start to close in. Romanian roads can be rough, with potholes after winter and the occasional unsigned speed trap near villages, so keep an eye on the surface and the speed limits, which are strictly enforced. A few dogs wander around and horse carts still use the shoulder. The reward is a ride that feels wild but never remote, with a village every few kilometres for coffee and a slice of papanasi, a fried doughnut served with sour cream and jam.
t.red lake@46.8,25.8:
Red Lake is a lake that should not exist, and the dead trees sticking out of the water tell you so. In the summer of 1837, a landslide off the flank of Mount Suhard dammed the Bicaz stream and the valley slowly filled behind it. The drowned spruces stayed standing and their pale trunks still rise from the water like a stand of masts. The name comes from the reddish clay that the stream washes down, though in practice the lake usually looks green, dark brown or blue-grey, depending on the weather and your angle.

It sits at around a thousand metres in the Hășmaș mountains, in a part of Transylvania where most people speak Hungarian and the lake is better known as Gyilkos-tó, the Murder Lake, a name that grew out of legends of shepherds drowned when the slope gave way. Local stories vary, and the legend is better known than any record of it, but it endures. The lake is shallow, cold, and a favourite for rowing boats and picnic stops.

The ride is the gorge. Coming up from the east side, the road threads Bicaz Gorge, a slot in the limestone where the walls rise some three hundred metres and the tarmac, a river and a few hairpin bends share a space that seems barely wide enough for one. Some of the best riding in Romania is in these few kilometres, but the stalls selling souvenirs at the top, the coaches, and the caravans of tourists in summer mean you should aim for an early start or a late afternoon. The surface can be rough and wet, and there are rockfalls after storms.

At the lake, expect stalls selling honey, jam, cheese and carved wooden items, plus cafes serving grilled meat, polenta and the local sweet cake called kürtőskalács, baked on a spit over coals. Fuel is not sold here, so use the larger town of Bălan, about sixteen kilometres away, or fill in the lowlands before the climb. Bring a warm layer, because mountain weather can turn quickly, and an early autumn day, with fog sitting in the hollows and golden beeches on the slopes, is hard to beat.
t.east london@-33.0,27.9:
East London is the only river port in South Africa, and the Buffalo River that runs through it has been the heart of the city since the nineteenth century. It began as a landing point for British troops during the frontier wars, grew into a harbour town, and today has nearly half a million people, a busy port, and a motor industry, with a large Mercedes-Benz plant. The city sits on the Indian Ocean coast of the Eastern Cape, with long, empty beaches such as Nahoon and Orient on its doorstep, and surf that draws bodyboarders and surfers all year.

The story that everyone tells is the coelacanth. In December 1938, a young museum curator named Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted a strange blue fish on the deck of a fishing trawler that had come into the harbour, and recognised it as something extraordinary. It turned out to be a coelacanth, a species thought to have died out with the dinosaurs, and her find astonished the scientific world. The East London Museum still tells the story, and it also holds the only intact dodo egg in the world, a quirky but true piece of trivia.

For motorcyclists, East London is the gateway to the Wild Coast. The N2 runs north-east through the former Transkei in long, rolling sections, with the sea always somewhere to the east, and side roads wander down to river mouths and small settlements. Livestock on the road is the main hazard, cattle, goats, pigs and dogs wander across freely, and villages have speed bumps that appear without warning. Summer is humid, with sudden storms, and winter is mild and dry, so it is a year-round destination, though the fierce south-westerly wind can be strong.

The city has every kind of service, with fuel stations on all the main roads, motorcycle dealers, banks, and a wide choice of food, from seafood on the waterfront to curries and braais. Spend an evening on the beachfront, where the sea breeze takes the edge off the heat, and check your bike over before heading into the quieter country beyond, where the distances between towns grow longer.
t.coffee bay@-32.0,29.1:
Coffee Bay gets its name from a shipwreck, or so the story goes. In the nineteenth century, a vessel carrying coffee beans is said to have gone down off this coast, and the beans washed ashore and sprouted on the beach, giving the place its name. Whatever the truth, the village is a small, laid-back settlement on the Wild Coast of the Eastern Cape, in the heart of the Xhosa homeland, with a crescent of sand, green hills and round thatched huts dotted over the slopes.

The coast is rugged and beautiful. A short distance away stands the Hole in the Wall, a huge rock arch in an island of dolerite, pierced by the sea, which the Xhosa call Izingolweni, the place of thunder, because of the noise the waves make as they rush through. Beaches run in long, empty strips, rivers meet the ocean at lagoons, and the hills behind are covered in grass and patches of forest. Hikers walk the coast from village to village, staying in simple lodges, and surfers come for the waves.

The ride in from the main road is a lesson in rural South Africa. After leaving the national road near Mthatha, the route winds over steep green hills on a road that is tarred but often scarred with potholes, with goats, cows and children on the carriageway and villages where people wave as you pass. Take it slowly, never ride at night, and watch for animals around blind bends. The mist rolls in from the sea in the mornings, and summer rain can make the road slick, so choose a dry day if you can.

Mthatha, the nearest large town and the place to stock up on fuel and supplies, is some way inland, and there is no reliable fuel in the village, so arrive with a full tank. The village has a couple of backpacker lodges and a few small shops, and a local cook will usually be glad to prepare fresh fish or a pot of stew if you ask in advance. The cultural life is lively, with Xhosa people in beaded costumes at weekends, and respect for local customs, such as asking before taking photographs, goes a long way. The night sky is dazzling.
t.matatiele@-30.3,28.8:
Matatiele sits on the South African side of the Drakensberg, in the far north-east of the Eastern Cape, and it is a small, tidy farming town in a land of rolling grass hills. The name comes from Sesotho and is usually translated as the ducks have flown away, a reference to the wetlands nearby, which attract waterbirds and cranes, including the endangered wattled crane. The Cape Drakensberg rises to the north-west, with snow in winter and wide views across the plateau, and the town sits at about 1,500 metres, so evenings are cool.

The region is a cross-border one. Lesotho lies a short distance to the west, and the town of Qacha's Nek, the border post and a small administrative centre, is about twenty-eight kilometres away, on the other side of the line. The two places are linked by a road that climbs steadily into the mountains, with the border crossing at a high saddle, and many of the people on either side are Basotho, so you will hear Sesotho and see the blankets and conical hats. Farms around Matatiele raise cattle and sheep, apples and timber, and the area has long been a quiet backwater.

On the bike, the ride to Qacha's Nek is a classic border route. The road is narrow, with bends and gradients, surfaces vary and conditions change, so ask locally, and the final approach to the border post, set at high altitude, brings great views over the Lesotho highlands, though mist and cold are a regular feature. Livestock on the road and sudden rain can make for slow going, and the gravel roads in Lesotho beyond demand more care. Allow time for the border, with passports, vehicle papers and sometimes a temporary import permit, and keep copies of everything.

Matatiele has fuel stations, shops, banks and a few guesthouses and cafés, and it is a sensible place to prepare for the mountains. The best months for riding are autumn and spring, with clear skies and dry roads, and the grass is golden in winter, with snow on the high peaks. Stock up on water and snacks, and fill the tank before crossing, since fuel in the Lesotho highlands is limited. A pie and a cup of coffee at a local café is a good way to start the day.
